meta.title: Attention Is All You Need
meta.summary: The paper introduces the **Transformer**, a neural network for turning one sequence into another (such as an English sentence into German) that drops the recurrent and convolutional layers then standard in the field and relies only on *attention*, a mechanism that lets every word look directly at every other word. The authors argue that recurrent networks are slow to train because they must process words one after another, whereas attention handles all positions at once and links distant words in a single step. They back this with a design analysis comparing layer types on cost, parallelism and path length, and with experiments: new state-of-the-art translation scores on two standard benchmarks at a fraction of competitors' training cost, an ablation study showing which components matter, and a strong result on a different task, sentence parsing. The architecture it describes became the basis of almost all later large language models.
meta.field: machine learning (natural language processing: neural machine translation)

outline.heading: Attention Is All You Need
outline.gist: Title and front matter: where the paper appeared, its eight authors and their affiliations, and a footnote saying who contributed what.

outline.heading: Abstract
outline.gist: Proposes the Transformer, built from attention alone, and headlines its translation scores, its low training cost and its success on parsing.

outline.heading: 1 Introduction
outline.gist: Recurrent networks dominate sequence tasks but compute one step at a time, which blocks parallel training; attention already helps but is bolted onto recurrence, so the paper proposes dropping recurrence altogether.

outline.heading: 2 Background
outline.gist: Places the work against convolutional models that also tried to cut sequential computation and against earlier uses of self-attention, and claims the Transformer is the first transduction model built on self-attention alone.

outline.heading: 3 Model Architecture
outline.gist: Keeps the familiar encoder–decoder design but builds both halves from stacked attention and feed-forward layers.

outline.heading: 3.1 Encoder and Decoder Stacks
outline.gist: Describes the six-layer encoder and decoder, their sub-layers, the residual connections and layer normalisation around each, and the masking that stops the decoder seeing words it has not yet produced.

outline.heading: 3.2 Attention
outline.gist: Defines attention in general: an output is a weighted average of values, with each weight set by how well a query matches the corresponding key.

outline.heading: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
outline.gist: Gives the paper's attention formula and argues for dividing the dot products by √dₖ so that the softmax does not saturate and stall learning.

outline.heading: 3.2.2 Multi-Head Attention
outline.gist: Splits attention into eight smaller heads running in parallel, so the model can attend to different kinds of information at once for about the cost of one full-size head.

outline.heading: 3.2.3 Applications of Attention in our Model
outline.gist: Lists the three places attention is used: encoder–decoder attention, self-attention in the encoder, and masked self-attention in the decoder.

outline.heading: 3.3 Position-wise Feed-Forward Networks
outline.gist: Adds a small two-layer network, applied to each position separately, inside every encoder and decoder layer.

outline.heading: 3.4 Embeddings and Softmax
outline.gist: Explains how tokens are turned into vectors and back into word probabilities, with one weight matrix shared between the embeddings and the output layer.

outline.heading: 3.5 Positional Encoding
outline.gist: Because attention by itself ignores word order, adds sine-and-cosine position signals to the inputs, and reports that learned position embeddings work about as well.

outline.heading: 4 Why Self-Attention
outline.gist: Compares self-attention with recurrent and convolutional layers on cost per layer, parallelism and the path length between distant words (Table 1), and suggests attention may also be easier to interpret.

outline.heading: 5 Training
outline.gist: Introduces the training set-up.

outline.heading: 5.1 Training Data and Batching
outline.gist: Describes the WMT 2014 English–German and English–French datasets, the subword vocabularies, and batching sentences of similar length together.

outline.heading: 5.2 Hardware and Schedule
outline.gist: Training used one machine with eight P100 GPUs: 12 hours for the base model and 3.5 days for the big one.

outline.heading: 5.3 Optimizer
outline.gist: Uses the Adam optimiser with a learning rate that rises for the first 4,000 steps and then decays.

outline.heading: 5.4 Regularization
outline.gist: Describes the measures against over-fitting, dropout and label smoothing (it announces three types but describes two).

outline.heading: 6 Results
outline.gist: Opens the results: translation, model variations and parsing.

outline.heading: 6.1 Machine Translation
outline.gist: The big Transformer sets new state-of-the-art BLEU scores on both translation benchmarks at a fraction of its rivals' training cost (Table 2).

outline.heading: 6.2 Model Variations
outline.gist: An ablation study that varies the number of heads, key size, model size, dropout and positional encoding to show which design choices matter (Table 3).

outline.heading: 6.3 English Constituency Parsing
outline.gist: Tests whether the model generalises beyond translation: with little tuning, it matches or beats most specialised parsers (Table 4).

outline.heading: 7 Conclusion
outline.gist: Restates the contribution and sets out future work: other kinds of data such as images and audio, restricted attention for long inputs, and less sequential generation.

outline.heading: References
outline.gist: The 40 cited works, numbered to match the bracketed citations in the text.

outline.heading: Attention Visualizations
outline.gist: Captions for appendix figures in which individual attention heads appear to track long-distance dependencies, pronoun reference and sentence structure.

arguments.name: The Transformer: attention alone is enough
arguments.gloss: The paper's central claim is that a translation model needs neither recurrence nor convolution: attention alone can relate the words of a sentence, and doing so is both faster to train and more accurate. The case has two halves. A design argument says recurrent networks are inherently sequential while attention works on all positions at once; an empirical argument shows record translation scores at lower training cost, plus a good result on parsing.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: Recurrent models compute one position after another; this "inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples", which matters most for long sequences.

premises.label: P2
premises.text: Attention lets a model relate positions regardless of how far apart they are, but until now it has almost always been used alongside a recurrent network.

premises.label: P3
premises.text: A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, where a recurrent layer needs O(n), and it is cheaper per layer whenever the sentence length n is smaller than the representation size d.

premises.label: P4
premises.text: On WMT 2014 English–German the big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 BLEU above the best previous models including ensembles; even the base model beats them all at a fraction of the training cost.

premises.label: P5
premises.text: On WMT 2014 English–French the big model beats every previously published single model at less than a quarter of the previous best model's training cost.

premises.label: P6
premises.text: On English constituency parsing, with little task-specific tuning, it beats every previously reported model except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: A sequence transduction model based entirely on attention can replace recurrent and convolutional architectures, training significantly faster while setting a new state of the art in translation (¶152–153).

arguments.pressurePoints: The speed-up is in training: generation still produces one word at a time, as the authors concede when they list 'making generation less sequential' as future work (¶154). Self-attention's cost grows with the square of the sequence length (Table 1), so the complexity advantage holds only for inputs shorter than the model width, which is why long-document and image work later produced many 'efficient attention' variants. The cost comparisons rest on estimated FLOPs (GPU time × assumed throughput, ¶104) against systems tuned differently. And this version reports the English–French score as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but 41.0 in ¶102; at 41.0 the model would not beat the best ensembles, which may be why ¶102 speaks only of single models.

arguments.name: Three desiderata: why self-attention
arguments.gloss: Section 4 justifies the choice of self-attention by comparing it with recurrent and convolutional layers on three criteria: the computation each layer costs, how much of it can run in parallel, and how many steps a signal must take between two distant words. Self-attention needs only a constant number of steps for both parallelism and path length, and is cheaper per layer for sentence-length inputs. The comparison is analytical, summarised in Table 1, rather than experimental.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: The first two criteria are total computation per layer and how much computation can be parallelised, measured by the minimum number of sequential operations.

premises.label: P2
premises.text: The third is path length: the shorter the paths signals must travel between positions, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies.

premises.label: P3
premises.text: Self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, whereas a recurrent layer needs O(n); self-attention is also cheaper than recurrence when n is smaller than d, as it usually is for sentences split into word-pieces or byte-pairs.

premises.label: P4
premises.text: A single convolutional layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all positions; doing so needs a stack of O(n/k) layers (or O(logₖ(n)) with dilation), and convolutions cost more than recurrent layers by a factor of k.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: For typical sentence-length inputs, self-attention matches or beats recurrent and convolutional layers on all three criteria, and is clearly better on parallelism and path length.

arguments.pressurePoints: Path length is a proxy for learnability borrowed from analyses of gradient flow in recurrent networks ([12]); the paper does not test directly that shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn. The per-layer cost advantage depends on n < d, which fails for documents, images and audio; the authors themselves propose restricting attention to a neighbourhood for long inputs (¶70, ¶154). Table 1 also leaves out memory, and attention must store an n × n table of weights for every head.

arguments.name: Why scale by √dₖ
arguments.gloss: Attention scores are dot products between a query vector and key vectors, fed through a softmax. The authors argue that in high dimensions these dot products become large, which pushes the softmax to put almost all its weight on one item; in that regime the model barely learns, because the gradients are tiny. Dividing by the square root of the dimension keeps the scores in a workable range while keeping dot-product attention's speed.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient than additive attention in practice, because it can use highly optimised matrix multiplication code.

premises.label: P2
premises.text: But for larger dₖ, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention without scaling (Britz et al. [3]).

premises.label: P3
premises.text: If the components of a query and a key are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance dₖ, so it grows with the dimension.

premises.label: P4
premises.text: Large dot products push the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: Scaling the dot products by 1/√dₖ counteracts the effect, giving the speed of dot-product attention without the saturation that hurts it at large dimensions.

arguments.pressurePoints: The authors say only that they 'suspect' this is the cause, and they report no experiment comparing scaled and unscaled attention. The independence and unit-variance assumptions describe random vectors, not learned ones. Their own ablation hints that the dot product may be too crude a compatibility function (¶130), and later very large models have sometimes added normalisation of queries and keys because scaling alone did not keep attention scores stable.

arguments.name: Many small heads beat one big one
arguments.gloss: Instead of one attention operation over the full 512-dimensional vectors, the Transformer runs eight smaller ones side by side and combines their results. The argument is that one head must average everything it attends to into one blend, while several heads can each pick out a different relationship. Because each head is an eighth of the size, the total cost stays about the same.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: With a single attention head, averaging over attended positions inhibits attending to different kinds of information at once (the 'reduced effective resolution' noted in ¶16).

premises.label: P2
premises.text: Multi-head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

premises.label: P3
premises.text: With h = 8 heads of dimension 64, the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality.

premises.label: P4
premises.text: In the ablation, single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, though quality also drops with too many heads.

premises.label: P5
premises.text: Visualised heads appear to have learned to perform different tasks.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: Several smaller attention heads improve quality over one full-size head at no extra computational cost.

arguments.pressurePoints: The measured gain is modest (0.9 BLEU on a development set, from single runs with no reported variance), and too many heads also hurts, so the optimum is found by trial rather than predicted. Later pruning studies, such as Michel, Levy and Neubig's 'Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?' (2019), found that many heads in trained models can be removed with little loss. The claim that heads specialise rests on a few hand-picked visualisations.

arguments.name: The case for sinusoidal positional encodings
arguments.gloss: Attention treats its input as an unordered set, so the model must be told where each word sits. The authors add fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies to each word's vector, hoping this makes relative position ("three words back") easy to learn. Learned position vectors did just as well, so the tie is broken by a hope that fixed waves will cope better with sentences longer than any seen in training.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: Since the model contains no recurrence and no convolution, information about the position of tokens must be injected for it to use word order.

premises.label: P2
premises.text: With sinusoids of geometrically spaced wavelengths, for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos), which they hypothesised would let the model easily learn to attend by relative position.

premises.label: P3
premises.text: Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results (Table 3, row E).

premises.label: P4
premises.text: The sinusoidal version may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: Use the fixed sinusoidal encoding rather than learned position embeddings.

arguments.pressurePoints: Both reasons are hypotheses the paper does not test: it never checks whether the model actually uses relative positions or how it copes with longer inputs. Later work found that sinusoidal encodings extrapolate poorly beyond the training length, notably Press, Smith and Lewis's ALiBi paper ('Train Short, Test Long', 2021), and relative and rotary position schemes have since largely replaced them.

arguments.name: Attention as a window into the model
arguments.gloss: As a side benefit, the authors suggest that attention makes the model easier to understand, because you can look at which words each head attends to. Their appendix shows heads that seem to link a verb to a distant part of its phrase, resolve what 'its' refers to, and follow sentence structure. The claim is hedged: self-attention 'could' yield more interpretable models.

premises.label: P1
premises.text: Attention distributions can be inspected directly, and individual heads clearly learn to perform different tasks.

premises.label: P2
premises.text: Many heads attend from 'making' to the distant words completing 'making...more difficult'.

premises.label: P3
premises.text: Two heads are apparently involved in anaphora resolution, with very sharp attention from 'its'.

premises.label: P4
premises.text: Many heads exhibit behaviour that seems related to the structure of the sentence.

conclusion.label: C
conclusion.text: Self-attention could yield more interpretable models.

arguments.pressurePoints: The evidence is a few selected examples from one layer, read by eye. Jain and Wallace's 'Attention is not Explanation' (2019) argued that attention weights often fail to track which inputs actually drive a prediction, and Wiegreffe and Pinter's reply 'Attention is not not Explanation' (2019) disputed how far that holds. Weights in a single layer also ignore how information has already been mixed across earlier layers.

bnsc5m4.label: Where this text comes from
bnsc5m4.what: A provenance note: the paper appeared at NIPS 2017 (now called NeurIPS), and this copy is version 7 of the arXiv preprint, with its tables reproduced under Google's stated permission.
bnsc5m4.how: This is not part of the argument but tells you which version you are reading. Machine-learning papers are often revised on arXiv after the conference, so the version number matters: small figures can differ between versions, and this one has an internal inconsistency in the English-to-French score (see the note on the abstract).

signals.note: Identifies the exact preprint version; "v7" means it was revised six times after first posting.
Flags that the tables come from the original under a stated permission, not redrawn from scratch.

b1dlvqkn.label: Eight authors, equal billing
b1dlvqkn.what: The author list: eight researchers, mostly at Google Brain and Google Research, with one at the University of Toronto. Every name carries the equal-contribution asterisk.
b1dlvqkn.how: The symbols point to footnotes in ¶6–¶8. Marking all eight as equal contributors is unusual; in machine learning, first authorship usually signals who led the work, and this paper deliberately refuses that signal.

signals.note: The asterisk, repeated on every name, marks equal contribution (explained in ¶6).
The dagger points to ¶7: his work was done while at Google Brain, though his listed affiliation is Toronto.

bj7oqa6.label: Abstract: drop recurrence entirely
bj7oqa6.what: Existing translation models rely on recurrent or convolutional networks, usually with attention linking encoder and decoder. The paper proposes the Transformer, which uses attention alone, and reports that it translates better than previous systems while training much faster; it also works for parsing sentence structure.
bj7oqa6.how: The abstract runs the standard empirical-paper arc: the state of the field, the proposal, then headline numbers as evidence. The key claim is a subtraction ("solely", "entirely"): keep the attention component that already worked and throw away the rest. The results are framed on two axes at once, quality and cost, which is the paper's real selling point and is developed in §6.1 and Table 2.

signals.note: The core thesis: attention is not an add-on here but the whole mechanism.

signals.q: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
signals.note: States what is removed; the novelty lies as much in the subtraction as in anything added.
Strengthens the claim: a single model beats combinations of several models, which usually score higher.

signals.q: a small fraction of the training costs
signals.note: Shifts the comparison from accuracy to efficiency, the second leg of the case.

bj7oqa6.critique: The abstract gives the English-to-French score as 41.8, but ¶102 in the results reports 41.0 for the same model, so a careful reader should notice the paper disagrees with itself. The claim that it "generalizes well" rests on one extra task, parsing.

b1gg827w.label: Who did what
b1gg827w.what: The footnote explains the random author order and credits each person's contribution: Uszkoreit proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention, Shazeer proposed the key attention variants and the position encoding, and others built models and the tensor2tensor code library.
b1gg827w.how: A contributions statement like this is a convention for large collaborative papers, used to make credit legible when author order no longer does. It also quietly previews the paper's main technical components (scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, the parameter-free position representation) before they are defined in §3.

signals.note: Explicitly cancels the usual meaning of author order, where first author signals lead contributor.

signals.q: Jakob proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention
signals.note: Credits the paper's central idea to one person.
Refers to the sine-and-cosine positional encoding of §3.5, which has no learned parameters.

b1hvtjrp.label: Affiliation note
b1hvtjrp.what: Aidan Gomez did this work while at Google Brain, even though his listed affiliation is the University of Toronto.
b1hvtjrp.how: A standard affiliation footnote that separates where the work was done from where the author is now or is primarily based.

signals.q: Work performed while at Google Brain.
signals.note: Separates where the work was done from the listed affiliation.

b3tu7sx.label: Affiliation note
b3tu7sx.what: Illia Polosukhin did this work while at Google Research.
b3tu7sx.how: The same kind of affiliation footnote, explaining why his name in ¶3 has no institution beside it.

signals.q: Work performed while at Google Research.
signals.note: Records where the work was done, since no institution is listed next to his name in ¶3.

b1gyem28.label: Publication venue
b1gyem28.what: The paper was published at the 31st NIPS conference, held in Long Beach, California, in 2017.
b1gyem28.how: A venue line. In machine learning, peer-reviewed conferences such as NIPS are the main publication outlets, carrying the prestige that journals carry in most other fields.

signals.q: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
signals.note: Names the venue; NIPS was renamed NeurIPS in 2018.

bg9iyaz.label: Recurrent networks rule translation
bg9iyaz.what: Recurrent neural networks, especially the LSTM and gated recurrent variants, are the established best approach for tasks that turn one sequence into another, such as translation and language modelling. Much recent work has tried to push them further.
bg9iyaz.how: The paper opens by granting the incumbent its standing, with a stack of citations as evidence of consensus. This sets up the contrast that the next paragraphs build: the approach is dominant but has a structural flaw. "Firmly established" concedes the opponent's strength so that replacing it looks more ambitious.

signals.q: firmly established as state of the art
signals.note: Grants the incumbent its full strength before challenging it.
Narrows "recurrent networks" to the two variants that actually work in practice, LSTM and GRU.
Frames the recent work as incremental improvement within the same paradigm.

b1t4owwc.label: The sequential bottleneck
b1t4owwc.what: Recurrent networks process a sequence one position at a time, each step waiting for the previous one. That makes it impossible to spread the work within one sentence across parallel hardware, which hurts most with long sequences. Tricks have made RNNs more efficient, but the basic limit remains.
b1t4owwc.how: This is the problem statement the whole paper answers. It moves from a description of how RNNs work (the hidden state at step t depends on step t−1) to a consequence ("precludes parallelization"), then concedes recent improvements before insisting they don't touch the root cause. The "however" in the last sentence carries the argument. §4 and Table 1 later formalise this as the O(n) sequential operations of a recurrent layer.

signals.note: The key inference: the dependency on the previous step is built in, so no engineering trick can remove it.
A scope limit: you can still process many sentences at once, just not the positions inside one.

signals.q: as memory constraints limit batching across examples
signals.note: Explains why the limit bites: the usual workaround, bigger batches, runs out of memory for long sequences.

signals.q: The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains.
signals.note: A concession-then-rebuttal: prior fixes are acknowledged, then declared insufficient.

b1t4owwc.critique: The argument is about training speed, not translation quality; RNNs' sequential nature could be argued to be a useful inductive bias for language, which this paragraph does not weigh.

b1o8h1tn.label: Attention works, but alongside RNNs
b1o8h1tn.what: Attention mechanisms, which let a model link any two positions regardless of how far apart they are, have become a standard part of the best sequence models. But almost always they are bolted on to a recurrent network.
b1o8h1tn.how: The paragraph isolates the component the paper will keep. Its first sentence praises attention for handling long distances; the second, turned on "however", points out that nobody has yet used it without recurrence. That gap is the opening for ¶14. The single exception [27] is honestly noted.

signals.note: Names attention's advantage: distance between words does not make them harder to connect.

signals.q: In all but a few cases [27], however,
signals.note: A hedge that admits a partial precedent (Parikh et al.) rather than claiming total novelty.

signals.q: in conjunction with a recurrent network
signals.note: Identifies the gap: attention has so far been an add-on, not the whole model.

b19sonkw.label: Proposal: the Transformer
b19sonkw.what: The paper proposes the Transformer, which drops recurrence and relies only on attention to link input and output. It parallelises far better and reaches a new state of the art in translation after as little as twelve hours of training on eight GPUs.
b19sonkw.how: This is the contribution statement, answering the problem in ¶12 with the ingredient praised in ¶13. "Eschewing" and "entirely" stress the radical subtraction. The twelve-hour figure refers to the smaller base model (§5.2), which already beats earlier English-to-German results according to Table 2; the headline scores in the abstract come from the big model trained for 3.5 days.

signals.note: A deliberate, emphatic verb: the absence of recurrence is the design choice, not an accident.

signals.q: relying entirely on an attention mechanism
signals.note: Restates the thesis in its strongest form.
A lower bound chosen for effect; it applies to the base model, not the one with the best scores.

b19sonkw.critique: "A new state of the art" after twelve hours holds for English-to-German with the base model; it is not true for English-to-French, where the base model scores 38.1 against earlier results above 40 (Table 2).

beouttk.label: Convolutional rivals and their cost
beouttk.what: Other attempts to cut sequential computation, such as the Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet and ConvS2S, use convolutional networks, which do process all positions in parallel. But linking two distant positions still takes more operations the further apart they are, which makes long-range relationships harder to learn. The Transformer makes this a constant, at a cost it then offsets with multi-head attention.
beouttk.how: The paragraph shows that its goal is shared by rivals, then distinguishes the Transformer on one measure: how many steps it takes to connect distant positions. It borrows the premise from [12] that shorter paths make dependencies easier to learn. Unusually, it volunteers a weakness of its own design ("albeit at the cost of") and points ahead to §3.2 for the fix; the same comparison returns in §4 and Table 1.

signals.q: The goal of reducing sequential computation
signals.note: Positions the rivals as allies on the goal, so the contest is about means.

signals.q: linearly for Convs2S and logarithmically for ByteNet
signals.note: Grades the rivals precisely: ByteNet's dilated convolutions grow more slowly than ConvS2S's.

signals.q: reduced to a constant number of operations
signals.note: The key comparative claim: any two positions are one step apart.

signals.q: albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution
signals.note: A concession: averaging over many positions blurs detail, which the design must compensate for.

beouttk.critique: "Reduced effective resolution" is asserted rather than demonstrated here; the only related evidence is Table 3 rows (A), where one attention head does 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting.

b108thu3.label: What self-attention is
b108thu3.what: Self-attention (also called intra-attention) is attention applied within a single sequence: each position looks at the other positions of the same sequence to build a representation of it. It has already worked well in reading comprehension, summarisation, entailment and sentence-representation tasks.
b108thu3.how: A definition followed by evidence of prior success, establishing that the paper's key ingredient is not new. This matters for reading the novelty claim in ¶19: what is new is using self-attention alone, not self-attention itself. The four citations spread the precedent across several tasks.

signals.note: Notes a synonym, useful because the earlier literature (e.g. [4]) uses that name.

signals.q: relating different positions of a single sequence
signals.note: The defining feature: contrast with encoder-decoder attention, which links two different sequences.
Establishes precedent; the paper does not claim to have invented self-attention.

b1fg5xw0.label: Memory networks as precedent
b1fg5xw0.what: End-to-end memory networks use a recurrent form of attention, repeating attention steps, rather than recurrence along the sequence, and they have done well on simple question-answering and language-modelling tasks.
b1fg5xw0.how: A further piece of related work, cited as a precedent for attention doing the heavy lifting without an RNN marching along the sequence. The contrast "instead of sequence-aligned recurrence" introduces a distinction that ¶19 reuses: recurrence as such is not the target, only recurrence that steps through positions one at a time. The scope limit "simple-language" keeps the precedent modest.

signals.q: recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence-aligned recurrence
signals.note: Separates two kinds of recurrence: repeating attention steps versus stepping through the sequence.
A scope limit that keeps the precedent from looking like a full rival on translation.

b11h98qq.label: Novelty claim and roadmap
b11h98qq.what: As far as the authors know, the Transformer is the first transduction model to rely entirely on self-attention, with no sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution. The rest of the paper will describe it, justify self-attention, and compare it with models like the Neural GPU, ByteNet and ConvS2S.
b11h98qq.how: The paragraph turns the survey of related work into a priority claim, hedged with "to the best of our knowledge". Its precision is deliberate: "first transduction model" and "relying entirely" are the qualifiers that make it true given the precedents in ¶13, ¶17 and ¶18. It closes with a signpost to §3 (the architecture) and §4 (why self-attention).

signals.q: To the best of our knowledge
signals.note: A standard hedge on a priority claim, protecting against an overlooked precedent.

signals.q: the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention
signals.note: The precise novelty claim; each qualifier excludes an earlier partial precedent.

signals.q: without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution
signals.note: Echoes ¶18's distinction, so only step-by-step recurrence is ruled out.
Signpost to the structure of the rest of the paper.

b1j3s679.label: The encoder-decoder template
b1j3s679.what: Most strong sequence-to-sequence models share a structure: an encoder turns the input symbols into a sequence of continuous vectors, and a decoder uses those vectors to produce the output one symbol at a time, feeding each output back in to generate the next.
b1j3s679.how: The paragraph defines the standard framework the Transformer inherits, so that the paper's innovation can be located inside it rather than replacing it. It is stated semi-formally: x₁…xₙ for input symbols, z for the encoder's vectors, y₁…yₘ for output symbols (m may differ from n). The "auto-regressive" property matters later, because the decoder's self-attention must be masked to preserve it (§3.2.3).

signals.q: Most competitive neural sequence transduction models
signals.note: A scope claim with citations, establishing the template as standard.
Marks the one place sequential processing survives: generation, not training.
A technical term: each output depends on the outputs already produced.

b1j3s679.critique: The paragraph quietly shows that the Transformer is not fully parallel: at generation time the decoder still works one word at a time, a limit the conclusion (¶154) admits as future work.

b27u6ph.label: Figure 1: the architecture
b27u6ph.what: The caption for Figure 1, the diagram of the whole Transformer: the encoder stack on the left and the decoder stack on the right.
b27u6ph.how: A figure caption. This copy does not reproduce the diagram, so ¶23 and §3.1–3.5 carry its content in words.

signals.note: Labels the figure as the architecture's overview, the reference point for the rest of §3.

bq68dfx.label: Overview of the Transformer's layers
bq68dfx.what: The Transformer keeps the encoder-decoder layout, building both halves from stacked self-attention layers and simple fully connected layers applied to each position separately.
bq68dfx.how: A bridging sentence that fits the new model into the template of ¶21 and names its two building blocks, which §3.1 to §3.3 then describe in detail. "Follows this overall architecture" stresses continuity: the novelty is in the parts, not the overall plan.

signals.note: Stresses continuity with the standard design of ¶21.

signals.q: stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers
signals.note: Names the two building blocks, expanded in §3.2 and §3.3.

signals.q: left and right halves of Figure 1
signals.note: Maps the prose onto the figure: encoder left, decoder right.

bme2am7.label: Encoder: six identical layers
bme2am7.what: The encoder is a pile of six identical layers. Each layer has two parts: a multi-head self-attention step and a small feed-forward network. Each part is wrapped in a "residual connection" (its input is added back to its output) and then normalised, and every part outputs vectors of the same width, 512 numbers.
bme2am7.how: This is a flat specification, not an argument: it states choices (six layers, width 512) without defending them here. The phrase "That is" converts the prose description into a compact formula, LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), which is the one precise claim in the paragraph. The final sentence gives the only stated rationale: the uniform width exists so that residual additions line up. Both sub-layers are only named here and are defined later, in 3.2 (attention) and 3.3 (feed-forward).

signals.note: Fixes a hyperparameter by stipulation. "Identical" means same design, not shared weights; each layer learns its own parameters.

signals.q: That is, the output of each sub-layer is
signals.note: Signals a restatement: the prose is now pinned down as an exact formula, which is what an implementer would follow.
Gives the purpose behind the fixed width of 512: you can only add x to Sublayer(x) if they have the same size.

bme2am7.critique: Why six layers and width 512 is not argued here; the only support is the later ablation in Table 3 rows (C). The placement of normalisation after the residual addition ("post-norm") was later widely replaced by normalising before each sub-layer ("pre-norm"), which tends to train more stably in deep stacks.

bek3e0g.label: Decoder adds cross-attention and masking
bek3e0g.what: The decoder is also six identical layers, but each has a third part that attends to the encoder's output, which is how the output side consults the input sentence. Its self-attention is also "masked" so that, when predicting word i, it cannot peek at words that come after i.
bek3e0g.how: Built as a contrast with ¶25: "also", "In addition to" and "Similar to the encoder" mark what carries over and what is new. The last sentence is a guarantee: two mechanisms together (masking plus shifting the outputs by one) are presented as jointly sufficient for the property that each prediction uses only earlier outputs. The mechanics of the third sub-layer and the mask are deferred to 3.2.3 (¶45 and ¶47).

signals.q: In addition to the two sub-layers
signals.note: Frames the decoder as the encoder plus one extra component, so the reader only has to learn the difference.

signals.q: to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions
signals.note: States the purpose of the mask: no looking ahead at words not yet generated.
The second half of the guarantee: the decoder's input is the target sentence shifted one step, so position i is fed the word before it and must predict word i.

signals.q: ensures that the predictions for position i
signals.note: A strong claim of sufficiency: masking plus the offset together rule out any leakage of future words.

bek3e0g.critique: The "offset by one" is doing essential work but gets half a clause; newcomers would need to know the standard practice of starting the decoder input with a start symbol and shifting the target right. The paragraph also does not note that this lets training run in parallel over all positions while generation at test time is still one word at a time.

byn9845.label: Attention as query–key–value lookup
byn9845.what: Attention in general takes a query and a collection of key–value pairs and produces an output. The output is a weighted average of the values, and each value's weight depends on how well the query matches that value's key.
byn9845.how: A general, abstract definition that sets up a template the next subsections fill in. "Can be described as" presents this as one useful way to see attention rather than the only one. The unspecified "compatibility function" is a slot: ¶31 fills it with a scaled dot product and ¶34 names the main alternative.

signals.note: Presents the definition as a redescription of a familiar mechanism in cleaner, more general terms.
The core idea: the output is a blend of values, not a single chosen one, so attention is a soft lookup.
Leaves the scoring method open on purpose; later paragraphs choose it.

byn9845.critique: The query/key/value vocabulary borrows from database or dictionary lookup, but the analogy is left unstated, which makes this paragraph harder than it needs to be for newcomers. It also leaves implicit that the weights are normalised to sum to one.

b2er88n.label: Figure 2: the two attention diagrams
b2er88n.what: The caption for Figure 2: the left panel shows scaled dot-product attention, the right panel shows multi-head attention, which runs several attention operations side by side.
b2er88n.how: A caption that points to diagrams explained in the next paragraphs: the left panel goes with ¶31–¶33 and the right with ¶37–¶41. "Running in parallel" previews the multi-head design and echoes the paper's wider theme of parallel computation.

signals.q: consists of several attention layers running in parallel
signals.note: Previews the key point of 3.2.2: several independent attention operations at once, not one after another.

b1voaqtg.label: Naming scaled dot-product attention
b1voaqtg.what: The paper names its specific version "Scaled Dot-Product Attention". It scores each query against each key by a dot product, divides the score by the square root of the key length, and turns the scores into weights with a softmax.
b1voaqtg.how: "We call" marks a naming stipulation, and the recipe that follows fills the "compatibility function" slot left open in ¶28. The steps are listed in the order they are computed. The one unusual step, dividing by √dₖ, is stated without justification; the reason comes in ¶35.

signals.note: Explicit naming: the authors coin a label for their variant, which the rest of the paper uses.
The distinctive step that separates this from plain dot-product attention; its rationale is deferred to ¶35.
Turns raw scores into positive weights that sum to one.

buvq6me.label: Batch the queries into matrices
buvq6me.what: In practice all queries are handled at once by stacking them as rows of a matrix Q, and likewise the keys into K and the values into V. The paragraph leads into the formula in ¶33.
buvq6me.how: "In practice" shifts from the conceptual one-query-at-a-time description to how it is actually computed. Packing into matrices is what lets the computation run as a few large matrix multiplications, which is central to the speed claims in ¶34 and section 4. The colon hands off to the equation.

signals.note: Marks a move from definition to implementation; nothing changes mathematically, only how it is computed.

signals.q: packed together into a matrix Q
signals.note: Stacking many vectors into one matrix lets hardware such as GPUs process them all in one operation.

bg5ffmp.label: Equation 1: the attention formula
bg5ffmp.what: The whole attention step in one line: multiply the queries by the transposed keys to get every query–key score, divide by √dₖ, apply softmax to each row to get weights, then use those weights to blend the values.
bg5ffmp.how: A displayed equation that condenses ¶31 and ¶32. Reading from the inside out follows the computation: QKᵀ gives a table of scores (one row per query, one column per key); the division scales them; softmax normalises each row; multiplying by V takes the weighted averages. It is numbered (1) so later text can refer back to it.

signals.note: Each part matches a verbal step in ¶31: dot products, scaling, softmax, weighted sum of values.

b19xqixb.label: Dot-product versus additive attention
b19xqixb.what: The two usual ways of scoring are additive attention, which uses a tiny neural network, and dot-product attention, which is the paper's method minus the scaling. They cost about the same in theory, but dot-product is much faster and uses less memory in practice because it runs on highly optimised matrix-multiplication code.
b19xqixb.how: Positions the authors' choice within existing options: "identical to our algorithm, except for" makes their contribution a small modification of a known method. The argument for choosing it is practical, not theoretical: it concedes theoretical parity ("similar in theoretical complexity") and then wins on real-world speed, with "since" giving the reason. It sets up ¶35, which addresses the one case where additive attention was better.

signals.q: identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor
signals.note: Honest positioning: the novelty is only the scaling, which ¶35 must now justify.
A concession that the two do not differ on paper, moving the case onto practical grounds.

signals.q: much faster and more space-efficient in practice
signals.note: The decisive claim, resting on how well modern hardware and libraries handle matrix multiplication.
Introduces the reason for the practical advantage.

b19xqixb.critique: The speed and memory advantage is asserted, not measured in the paper; it is widely accepted, but no figures are given.

b1p1fmuz.label: Why scale by √dₖ
b1p1fmuz.what: Earlier work found that with long keys, additive attention beat unscaled dot-product attention. The authors suspect this is because dot products of long vectors get large, which pushes the softmax into a flat region where learning signals (gradients) are tiny; dividing by √dₖ keeps the scores in a workable range.
b1p1fmuz.how: Starts from an empirical finding credited to [3], then offers a causal explanation explicitly hedged with "We suspect", then the design fix introduced by "To counteract this effect". Footnote 1 (¶203) supports the hypothesis with a short calculation: if the parts of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance dₖ, so its typical size grows like √dₖ, which is exactly what the division cancels.

signals.q: additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling
signals.note: The empirical premise the fix responds to; note "without scaling" narrows the comparison precisely.
A hedge: the mechanism is offered as a plausible explanation, not something they tested directly.
The feared failure: when softmax saturates, small changes in the scores barely change its output, so training slows or stalls.
Presents the scaling as a remedy aimed at the hypothesised cause.

b1p1fmuz.critique: No experiment in the paper isolates the effect of the scaling (Table 3 does not remove it), so the explanation rests on the footnote's idealised assumptions. Later, ¶130 even suggests the dot product may be too simple a compatibility function.

b1qk0vpl.label: Several smaller attentions, then combine
b1qk0vpl.what: Rather than one attention over full-width vectors, the model makes h different, learned, lower-dimensional versions of the queries, keys and values, runs attention on each in parallel, joins (concatenates) the results, and projects them back to full width.
b1qk0vpl.how: "Instead of" sets up a contrast with the obvious single-attention design; "we found it beneficial" gives an empirical rather than theoretical justification. The steps are listed in computational order (project, attend, concatenate, project) and point to Figure 2 (right) and the formulas in ¶39–¶41. The evidence behind "beneficial" is Table 3 rows (A), discussed in ¶129.

signals.q: Instead of performing a single attention function
signals.note: Frames multi-head attention as a replacement for the default one-head design.
The justification is empirical and mildly hedged: it worked better in their experiments.
Each head gets its own learned view of the inputs, so heads can pick out different information.
How the heads are recombined into a single output of the usual width.

bsv81xa.label: Why several heads help
bsv81xa.what: Several heads let the model look at different kinds of relationships at different positions at the same time. A single head has to average everything into one set of weights, which blurs these distinctions.
bsv81xa.how: A two-sentence rationale: a positive claim about what multi-head attention "allows", then a terse contrast ("averaging inhibits this"). It picks up the worry flagged in ¶16 about "reduced effective resolution due to averaging" and presents multiple heads as the answer. "Representation subspaces" is technical shorthand for the different lower-dimensional projections each head works in.

signals.q: allows the model to jointly attend
signals.note: A capability claim: the design makes something possible, not guaranteed.
Each head's projection is a different lower-dimensional "view" of the vectors, so heads can specialise.
The contrast case in three words: one softmax-weighted average cannot focus on several things at once.

bsv81xa.critique: This is asserted rather than shown; the support is the ablation in Table 3 (A) and the illustrative attention maps in the appendix (¶200–¶202). Later research found that many heads in trained Transformers can be removed with little loss, which complicates the picture of every head doing distinct work.

b1jev5r6.label: Multi-head formula: concatenate and project
b1jev5r6.what: The formula for multi-head attention: compute each head, place the head outputs side by side (Concat), then multiply by an output matrix Wᴼ to mix them back into one vector per position.
b1jev5r6.how: A displayed equation formalising the last step of ¶37. The individual heads are defined in the next line (¶40) and the matrix sizes in ¶41, so the three lines read as one definition.

signals.note: Joins the h head outputs end to end, then a learned matrix recombines them so heads can share information.

b17ls4sn.label: Each head is ordinary attention
b17ls4sn.what: Each head i is just the scaled dot-product attention of Equation 1, applied after multiplying Q, K and V by that head's own learned matrices.
b17ls4sn.how: Defines the term used in ¶39 with a "where" clause, reusing Attention(…) from ¶33, so the new mechanism is built entirely from the old one plus learned projections.

signals.q: Attention(Q Wᵢ^Q, K Wᵢ^K, V Wᵢ^V)
signals.note: The only difference between heads is the projection matrices Wᵢ; the attention computation is the same.

b1l60qkw.label: Sizes of the projection matrices
b1l60qkw.what: Specifies the shapes of the learned matrices: each head's query and key projections shrink d_model-wide vectors to dₖ, the value projection to dᵥ, and the output matrix maps the h joined heads (h·dᵥ wide) back to d_model.
b1l60qkw.how: A continuation of the "where" clauses in ¶39–¶40 that fixes dimensions. The notation W ∈ ℝ^(a × b) means W is a table of real numbers with a rows and b columns. These shapes are what make the cost claim in ¶42 work.

signals.note: "Parameter" means these numbers are learned in training, not fixed by hand.
The output matrix takes the concatenated heads back to the model's standard width, so the next layer sees the usual size.

b13hj578.label: Eight heads of width 64
b13hj578.what: The model uses 8 heads, each working with 64-number vectors (512 divided by 8). Because each head is smaller, the total cost is about the same as one full-width head.
b13hj578.how: "In this work we employ" marks a configuration choice for this model rather than a general claim. "Due to" introduces the cost argument: splitting 512 dimensions into 8 × 64 keeps the total amount of computation roughly unchanged, so extra heads come almost free. Table 3 rows (A) later vary h while holding this cost constant.

signals.note: Scopes the numbers to this model; other settings are explored in Table 3.
The width is divided among the heads, not multiplied, which is the key to the cost claim.

signals.q: similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality
signals.note: The cost-neutrality claim: multi-head attention does not buy its benefits with more computation.

b13hj578.critique: "Similar" is approximate: the extra output projection Wᴼ adds some cost, though small relative to the rest.

bz32gkt.label: Three uses of attention
bz32gkt.what: Announces that multi-head attention is used in three places in the model, listed in the next three paragraphs.
bz32gkt.how: A one-line signpost that organises ¶45–¶47 as an enumerated list: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention and decoder self-attention.

signals.note: Sets up a three-part list, telling the reader how the following paragraphs are structured.

b1cqo6xn.label: Encoder-decoder (cross) attention
b1cqo6xn.what: In the decoder's middle sub-layer, the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder's output. So each output position can look at every word of the input sentence, as in earlier translation models.
b1cqo6xn.how: Specifies where Q, K and V come from, which is all that distinguishes the three uses. "This allows" states the consequence, and "This mimics" ties the design to the attention used in earlier sequence-to-sequence systems [38, 2, 9], presenting this part as continuity rather than novelty. It fills in the third sub-layer introduced in ¶26.

signals.q: the queries come from the previous decoder layer
signals.note: The decoder asks the questions; this is what makes it cross-attention rather than self-attention.
"Memory" casts the encoder output as a store the decoder looks things up in.

signals.q: This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms
signals.note: Positions this component as borrowed from established practice, not new.

b1psr8i5.label: Encoder self-attention
b1psr8i5.what: In the encoder's self-attention, queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer's output. Every position can attend to every other position, in both directions.
b1psr8i5.how: Defines self-attention by the source of its inputs ("from the same place"), and gives the scope of connection ("all positions"). The unrestricted scope contrasts with the masked decoder in ¶47, and is the basis of the constant path length argued for in section 4.

signals.q: all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place
signals.note: The defining feature of self-attention: a sequence attending to itself.
No restriction or mask in the encoder: each word sees the whole sentence, earlier and later.

b91cgu6.label: Masked decoder self-attention
b91cgu6.what: The decoder's self-attention only lets each position look at itself and earlier positions. This is done by setting the scores for later positions to minus infinity before the softmax, which makes their weights exactly zero.
b91cgu6.how: "Similarly" links to ¶46, then a scope limit ("up to and including") marks the difference. "We need to... to preserve" gives the purpose: the model generates text left to right (auto-regressively, as defined in ¶21), so it must not use words it has not yet produced. The implementation detail explains how the promise made in ¶26 is kept.

signals.q: up to and including that position
signals.note: The exact scope limit: the current position and all earlier ones, nothing later.
Gives the reason: at test time the model produces one word at a time, so training must not let it see the future.
The trick: softmax turns −∞ into a weight of zero, so masked positions contribute nothing.
Normative wording: connections to later positions would be cheating, not just unhelpful.

b91cgu6.critique: "Leftward information flow" means information from later positions flowing back to earlier ones, which can confuse readers picturing the sentence differently. The mask makes training parallel, but generation remains step by step, a limitation ¶154 acknowledges.

b7jve1y.label: Per-position feed-forward network
b7jve1y.what: Besides attention, every encoder and decoder layer has a small neural network applied to each position on its own, the same way at every position. It is two linear transformations with a ReLU in between.
b7jve1y.how: "In addition to" places this as the second sub-layer promised in ¶25. "Separately and identically" is the key specification: attention mixes information across positions, and this network then processes each position independently. The formula follows in ¶50.

signals.q: applied to each position separately and identically
signals.note: No information passes between positions here; that job belongs to attention.

signals.q: two linear transformations with a ReLU activation
signals.note: The standard minimal neural network: a linear map, a simple non-linearity, another linear map.

bu65q57.label: Equation 2: the feed-forward formula
bu65q57.what: The feed-forward network as a formula: multiply by W₁ and add b₁, replace any negative numbers with zero (the ReLU), then multiply by W₂ and add b₂.
bu65q57.how: A displayed equation that makes ¶49 exact. The max(0, …) is the ReLU; W₁, W₂ are learned weight matrices and b₁, b₂ learned offsets (biases).

signals.note: This is the ReLU: keep positive values, set negatives to zero. It supplies the non-linearity that lets the network represent more than straight-line relationships.

b15l9l8e.label: Shared across positions, not layers
b15l9l8e.what: The feed-forward weights are the same at every position within a layer but differ between layers. The operation can also be described as two convolutions with kernel size 1. Its input and output are 512 wide and its hidden layer is 2,048 wide.
b15l9l8e.how: "While... they use different parameters" draws a distinction about what is shared. "Another way of describing this" offers a redescription in convolutional-network terms, helpful to readers from that tradition and a reminder that the paper does not use convolution in the usual sense. The sizes fix the configuration: the inner layer is four times wider than the model width.

signals.note: Weight sharing across positions, just like a convolution sliding over a sequence.

signals.q: different parameters from layer to layer
signals.note: Each of the six layers learns its own feed-forward weights.
Marks an equivalent redescription, not a new mechanism.
The inner width, four times d_model; Table 3 rows (C) try other values.

b15l9l8e.critique: The paper gives no rationale for the feed-forward layer's role or for the fourfold expansion; its importance is supported only by the size variations in Table 3.

b1sj9600.label: Tied embeddings and output layer
b1sj9600.what: Words (strictly, sub-word tokens) are turned into lists of 512 numbers by a learned lookup table, and at the other end the decoder's output is turned back into a probability for each possible next token. The authors reuse one matrix of weights for all three jobs: the encoder's input lookup, the decoder's input lookup and the final output layer. They also scale the looked-up vectors up by √d_model (about 22.6).
b1sj9600.how: Most of the paragraph is framed as standard practice ("Similarly to other…", "the usual…"), which tells the reader these choices are inherited, not claimed as contributions. The one borrowed twist, sharing weights, is credited to Press and Wolf [30]. The √d_model scaling is simply stated, with no reason given. Sharing one matrix between encoder and decoder only works because the source and target languages use a single shared vocabulary, which ¶76 confirms.

signals.q: Similarly to other sequence transduction models
signals.note: Marks what follows as conventional, so the reader should not look for novelty here.
Credits the weight-sharing idea to earlier work while signalling a small variation (they share across both embedding layers as well as the output layer).
A bare stipulation: no justification is offered, though it plausibly keeps the embeddings on a similar scale to the positional encodings added to them (¶61).

b1sj9600.critique: The scaling factor and the three-way weight sharing are never tested on their own; Table 3 has no row isolating either, so the reader must take their value on trust.

b1uinmgh.label: Table 1: cost comparison defined
b1uinmgh.what: This is the caption of Table 1, which compares four kinds of layer on three measures: how much computation each layer needs, how many steps must happen one after another, and how far information has to travel between two distant words. It defines the letters used: n is sentence length, d the size of each word's vector, k the width of a convolution window and r the size of a restricted attention window.
b1uinmgh.how: The table sits here because of page layout, but it is really the evidence for Section 4 (¶67–¶72), which walks through it row by row. The caption fixes the variables so that the comparison is purely in terms of how costs grow with n and d. Everything is stated in big-O notation, which ignores constant factors.

signals.note: Names the paper's own proxy for how easy it is to learn long-range dependencies, argued for in ¶69.
Operationalises 'parallelisable': steps that cannot run at the same time.
Introduces a variant the paper does not actually build; it appears only as a proposal in ¶70.

b1uinmgh.critique: Big-O figures hide constants and memory costs, so they show how costs scale rather than which layer is faster on real hardware at real sentence lengths.

b211o68.label: Table 1 column headings
b211o68.what: The table's three columns match the three desiderata of Section 4: total computation per layer, how many operations must run in sequence, and the longest path a signal travels between any two positions.
b211o68.how: The column order mirrors the order of the argument in ¶68–¶69, so the table works as a summary of the case for self-attention before the case is made. Each column is a worst-case growth rate rather than a measured time.

signals.note: Total work done by one layer, the first desideratum (¶68).
How many steps must wait for the previous one, the measure of parallelisability (¶68).
The third desideratum, tied to learning long-range dependencies (¶69).

blgece9.label: Self-attention: quadratic but instant
blgece9.what: Self-attention costs work proportional to n²·d, because every word is compared with every other word using d-dimensional vectors. But all those comparisons can happen at once (O(1) sequential steps), and any word can reach any other in a single hop (path length O(1)).
blgece9.how: This row carries the paper's central selling point: constant sequential steps and constant path length. The quadratic term in n is the price, and ¶70 argues it is affordable only under the condition that n is smaller than d.

signals.note: The quadratic dependence on sequence length: doubling the input length quadruples the work. This is the architecture's well-known weak point for long inputs.
Constant sequential steps and constant path length, the two columns where self-attention beats every alternative.

blgece9.critique: The O(n²) cost also applies to memory, which the table does not show; this became the main obstacle to applying Transformers to long documents, images and audio.

b1vzilvs.label: Recurrent layer: step by step
b1vzilvs.what: A recurrent layer processes the sentence one word at a time, so it needs n steps in sequence, and information from the first word must pass through every intermediate step to reach the last (path length O(n)). Its total work, n·d², comes from multiplying each word's d-sized state by a d×d matrix.
b1vzilvs.how: This is the row the paper is arguing against, since recurrent networks were the dominant approach (¶5). Its O(n) sequential steps is the bottleneck behind the claim that the Transformer trains faster; its O(n) path length connects to the vanishing-gradient literature cited in ¶69.

signals.note: Linear in sentence length but quadratic in vector size, the mirror image of self-attention's n²·d.
Both the sequential steps and the path length grow with sentence length, the two weaknesses the Transformer targets.

b14opgtz.label: Convolutional layer: logarithmic paths
b14opgtz.what: A convolutional layer looks at a window of k neighbouring words. All positions can be computed at once (O(1) sequential steps), but it takes several stacked layers for distant words to meet; with dilated convolutions the path length grows only with the logarithm of n.
b14opgtz.how: This row represents the other main rival, convolutional translation models such as ByteNet and ConvS2S (¶71, Table 2). It matches self-attention on parallelism, so the argument against it has to rest on cost (a factor of k more work) and path length.

signals.note: Like the recurrent layer's cost but multiplied by the window width k, the basis of ¶71's remark that convolutions are 'generally more expensive'.
Path length assuming dilated convolutions; ¶71 notes that plain contiguous windows would need O(n/k) layers instead.

b14opgtz.critique: The table quietly picks the most favourable path length for convolutions (dilated) but the plain cost for the layer, mixing assumptions within a single row.

b18o03a2.label: Restricted self-attention: a proposal
b18o03a2.what: If each word attends only to a window of r neighbours instead of the whole sentence, the work drops to r·n·d, linear in sentence length, but distant words are now n/r hops apart.
b18o03a2.how: This is a hypothetical row: the paper never trains such a model and defers it to future work in ¶70 and the Conclusion (¶154). It shows the authors anticipating the quadratic-cost objection and sketching a trade-off: cheaper computation for longer paths.

signals.note: Labels a design the paper describes but does not test.
The trade-off in one line: cost becomes linear in n, parallelism is kept, but path length grows again.

bj0hgrg.label: Why position must be added
bj0hgrg.what: Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it has no built-in sense of word order: to plain self-attention a sentence is just a set of words. So the authors add a 'positional encoding', a vector the same size as each word embedding, to every input embedding, to tell the model where each word sits.
bj0hgrg.how: The paragraph runs as a short necessity argument: the premise is what the model lacks ("Since…"), the conclusion is what must therefore be added ("we must inject"). The equal-dimension requirement is explained as a consequence of choosing to add rather than concatenate. It then concedes a design space ("many choices…, learned and fixed"), setting up the choice justified in ¶62–¶65.

signals.q: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution
signals.note: States the premise: order information came for free in the rival architectures, so its removal creates a gap.
Marks necessity, not preference; without it the model could not distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.

signals.q: so that the two can be summed
signals.note: Explains a design constraint by its purpose.

signals.q: There are many choices of positional encodings
signals.note: Concedes that the solution is not unique, which invites the comparison in ¶65.

bj0hgrg.critique: Why add the position vector rather than concatenate it is not argued; adding means word identity and position share the same numbers, a choice later work has questioned and revised.

bhcohwa.label: Sinusoidal encoding announced
bhcohwa.what: Introduces the specific choice: positions are encoded with sine and cosine waves of different frequencies.
bhcohwa.how: A one-line bridge from the general need (¶61) to the formula (¶63). "In this work" scopes the choice to this paper rather than presenting it as the right answer.

signals.note: Scope marker: a design decision for this paper, not a general claim.
The key idea in brief: each dimension oscillates at its own rate, so together they give each position a distinct pattern.

b1vv9i8j.label: The positional-encoding formula
b1vv9i8j.what: Each position pos gets a vector in which the even-numbered dimensions hold a sine wave and the odd-numbered ones a cosine wave. The frequency falls as the dimension index i rises, so early dimensions change quickly from word to word (like the second hand of a clock) and later ones very slowly (like the hour hand). The constant 10000 sets how slow the slowest wave is.
b1vv9i8j.how: A formal definition presented as an equation with no argument; the explanation follows in ¶64. The pairing of sine and cosine at the same frequency is what makes the relative-position property claimed in ¶64 hold.

signals.note: Even dimensions use sine.
Odd dimensions use cosine at the same frequency, forming sine–cosine pairs.
The divisor 10000^(2i/d_model) makes the wavelength grow geometrically across dimensions, from very short to very long.

b1vv9i8j.critique: The constant 10000 is not justified or varied in the experiments; it looks like a convenient choice rather than a tuned one.

ba4dnl4.label: Why sinusoids: relative position
ba4dnl4.what: The wavelengths run from 2π up to 10000·2π positions, spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale. The authors picked this scheme because shifting a position by a fixed amount k changes the encoding in a way that is a fixed linear transformation (in effect, rotating each sine–cosine pair). They hoped this would make it easy for the model to attend to words 'three to the left' and similar, regardless of absolute position.
ba4dnl4.how: The paragraph first glosses the formula ("That is…"), then gives the rationale, explicitly flagged as a hypothesis rather than a result. The mathematical property (the linear-shift fact) is true and stated without proof; the leap from 'can be represented linearly' to 'easy for the model to learn' is the hypothesised part.

signals.note: Signals a restatement in plainer terms of the formula in ¶63.

signals.q: The wavelengths form a geometric progression
signals.note: Each wavelength is a fixed multiple of the previous, so the encoding covers many scales, from neighbouring words to very distant ones.
An explicit hedge: this is the motivation for the design, not something the paper tests.

signals.q: can be represented as a linear function
signals.note: The mathematical fact the hypothesis rests on; attention layers are built from linear maps, so linear relationships are easy for them to exploit.

ba4dnl4.critique: No experiment checks whether the model actually uses relative positions in this way; ¶65 shows only that learned encodings do about as well.

bokeko4.label: Learned versus fixed: a tie
bokeko4.what: The authors also tried learning the position vectors from data, as ConvS2S [9] does, and got almost the same results (Table 3, row E: 25.7 BLEU against 25.8 for the base model). They kept the sinusoidal version because it might let the model handle sentences longer than any it saw in training.
bokeko4.how: A small ablation turns what could look like an arbitrary choice into a tie-break: since performance is equal, the choice is made on a secondary, speculative ground. The hedge "may allow" marks that ground as untested. This result connects to Table 3 row (E) in Section 6.2.

signals.note: Signals a robustness check on the design choice.
Concedes that the sinusoidal choice brings no measured gain.

signals.q: it may allow the model to extrapolate
signals.note: A hedged, untested advantage used as the tie-breaker.

bokeko4.critique: The extrapolation claim is never tested here, and later work on length extrapolation found that sinusoidal encodings in practice extrapolate poorly beyond training lengths, which motivated schemes such as relative and rotary position encodings.

b1i7xwgr.label: Setting up the comparison
b1i7xwgr.what: Section 4 compares self-attention layers with recurrent and convolutional layers as ways of turning one sequence of vectors into another of the same length, the core job inside any encoder or decoder. The comparison uses three desired properties.
b1i7xwgr.how: The paragraph frames the section openly as motivation ("Motivating our use of self-attention"), so what follows is advocacy for a design already chosen rather than a neutral survey. It defines the common task abstractly (x₁…xₙ to z₁…zₙ) so that all three layer types can be compared on equal terms.

signals.note: Admits the section's purpose: to justify a choice already made.

signals.q: one variable-length sequence of symbol representations
signals.note: Defines the shared job every candidate layer must do, making the comparison like-for-like.
Announces the criteria; the reader should ask whether they were chosen because attention does well on them.

b1i7xwgr.critique: The criteria are theoretical and asymptotic; they leave out memory use, constant factors and how well each layer type generalises, which a sceptic would want weighed too.

bdrxt9p.label: Criteria one and two
bdrxt9p.what: The first criterion is total computation per layer. The second is how much of that computation can be run in parallel, measured by the smallest number of steps that must be done one after another.
bdrxt9p.how: Two criteria are stated briskly as evaluation standards. The second is given a precise operational measure ("as measured by"), which lets Table 1's middle column stand in for the vague notion of parallelisability.

signals.note: The first desideratum: raw amount of work.

signals.q: as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations
signals.note: Operationalises parallelism, which matters because GPUs are fast only when work can run side by side.

bzasdvd.label: Short paths aid long-range learning
bzasdvd.what: The third criterion is path length. Learning relationships between far-apart words (say, a verb and its subject many words earlier) is hard, and a key reason is that the training signal must travel through many steps to link them. Shorter paths make such dependencies easier to learn, so the authors compare the longest path between any two positions.
bzasdvd.how: A compact chain of reasoning: a problem (long-range dependencies are hard), a cause ("One key factor"), a general principle backed by citation [12], then a conclusion about what to measure ("Hence"). The citation is to work on vanishing gradients in recurrent networks, so the principle is imported from RNNs and applied to all layer types.

signals.note: Establishes the problem as widely recognised.
Hedges: path length is one cause among others, not the only one.

signals.q: the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]
signals.note: The empirical-theoretical premise, borrowed from gradient-flow analysis of recurrent networks.
Marks the inference from the principle to the choice of metric.

bzasdvd.critique: Path length is a proxy; the paper does not show that the Transformer actually learns long-range dependencies better because of it, apart from the qualitative attention pictures in the appendix.

b1cer0uz.label: Self-attention beats recurrence here
b1cer0uz.what: Self-attention links all positions in a constant number of steps, whereas a recurrent layer needs n. It also does less total work than a recurrent layer whenever sentence length n is smaller than vector size d, which is usual in translation, where sentences are typically shorter than the 512-dimensional vectors (especially with sub-word units such as word-pieces [38] and byte-pairs [31]). For very long inputs, attention could be limited to a local window of r words, at the cost of longer paths (O(n/r)), which the authors leave for future work.
b1cer0uz.how: The argument reads Table 1 in two steps: an outright win on sequential operations, then a conditional win on computation (n²d beats nd² exactly when n < d). The condition is backed by an empirical claim about typical sentence lengths ("most often the case"). The paragraph then anticipates the obvious objection, long sequences, and answers it only with an untested proposal.

signals.q: whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n)
signals.note: The unconditional advantage, the heart of the speed claim.

signals.q: when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d
signals.note: A scope condition: the computational advantage holds only in this regime.

signals.q: which is most often the case
signals.note: An empirical hedge, true for sentence-level translation but not for long documents.

signals.q: We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.
signals.note: Defers the long-sequence problem rather than solving it; compare the Conclusion (¶154).

b1cer0uz.critique: The favourable condition n < d holds for sentences but fails for documents, code, images or audio, where n runs to thousands; the quadratic cost then dominates, as later research on efficient attention showed.

b1rnfml8.label: Convolutions: more layers, more cost
b1rnfml8.what: A single convolution with window k smaller than n cannot link every pair of words, so connecting everything needs a stack of about n/k layers, or log n with dilated convolutions [18], lengthening the paths. Convolutions also cost about k times more than recurrent layers. Separable convolutions [6] cut this cost, but even at their most expensive (k = n) they only match what the Transformer already spends on one self-attention layer plus one feed-forward layer.
b1rnfml8.how: The paragraph moves through a concession structure: it grants convolutions their best case (dilated, then separable) and argues each still falls short or merely ties. The closing "Even with k = n, however" turns a potential rival into a point of equivalence that favours the authors' design, since their layer pair buys full connectivity for the same price.

signals.q: does not connect all pairs of input and output positions
signals.note: The core weakness named: limited reach per layer.

signals.q: Convolutional layers are generally more expensive
signals.note: A general claim hedged by "generally"; the factor of k comes from the window width.
Concedes the strongest counter-case.
Turns the concession: the best convolutional option only equals the Transformer's cost.

b1rnfml8.critique: The comparison is purely asymptotic; it does not weigh how well each design actually learns, which is what Table 2's BLEU results address empirically.

bbagbq.label: Interpretability as a side benefit
bbagbq.what: An extra advantage: attention weights can be inspected to see which words the model is 'looking at'. The appendix shows examples (Figures 3–5) where different attention heads seem to have specialised, some tracking sentence structure or linking a pronoun to what it refers to.
bbagbq.how: Explicitly flagged as a secondary point ("As side benefit"), and hedged ("could yield", "appear to"). Yet the final sentence mixes a confident claim ("clearly learn") with a hedged one ("appear to exhibit"). The evidence is qualitative: selected pictures in the appendix (¶198–¶202).

signals.note: Signals that this is not part of the main case for the design.
A modal hedge: a possibility, not a demonstrated property.

signals.q: clearly learn to perform different tasks
signals.note: An unhedged claim resting on a few hand-picked visualisations.
Hedges the stronger claim that heads encode grammar and meaning.

bbagbq.critique: Whether attention weights explain a model's behaviour was later disputed (for example Jain and Wallace's 'Attention is not Explanation', 2019, and Wiegreffe and Pinter's reply, 2019); cherry-picked heat maps are weak evidence either way.

b1eh792r.label: Training section opens
b1eh792r.what: Announces that Section 5 describes how the models were trained.
b1eh792r.how: A one-sentence signpost. "Training regime" signals practical detail (data, hardware, optimiser, regularisation) that matters for reproducing the results rather than for the argument.

signals.note: Flags the practical recipe that follows in ¶76–¶86.

bfdvi6b.label: Data and batching
bfdvi6b.what: English–German training used the standard WMT 2014 dataset of about 4.5 million sentence pairs, broken into sub-word units by byte-pair encoding with one shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens for both languages. English–French used a much larger 36-million-sentence set and a 32,000-unit word-piece vocabulary. Sentences of similar length were grouped into batches of roughly 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens.
bfdvi6b.how: Pure method reporting. Calling the dataset "standard" signals that results are comparable with earlier work in Table 2.
