terms.inThisPaper: Input and output tokens are embedded as d_model-wide vectors (section 3.4), with positional encodings added. The "output embeddings" feed the decoder the target sentence shifted by one position. The two embedding tables and the final pre-softmax matrix share weights.

terms.short: Blocking certain positions from being attended to, by forcing their attention weights to zero.
terms.background: Masking is a general technique in sequence models, used both to ignore padding and, as here, to stop a model from seeing future tokens. "Causal" or "look-ahead" masking is the later common name for this second use.
terms.inThisPaper: In the decoder's self-attention, scores for later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, which makes their weights zero. With the one-position offset of the decoder inputs, this ensures predictions for position i depend only on earlier outputs, so training can run on the whole sentence in parallel.

terms.short: The three roles vectors play in attention: a query is compared with keys to decide weights, and those weights are applied to the values paired with the keys.
terms.background: The vocabulary borrows from databases and dictionaries, where a query is matched against keys to retrieve values; attention is a "soft" version that retrieves a blend rather than one item. Key-value memory networks (Miller et al., 2016) used the split before this paper, which made the terms standard.
terms.inThisPaper: Queries, keys and values are vectors, stacked into matrices Q, K and V. In self-attention all three come from the same layer; in encoder-decoder attention the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values (called "memory") from the encoder.

terms.short: The scoring rule that measures how well a query matches a key, determining that key's attention weight.
terms.background: Attention mechanisms differ mainly in this scoring function. Bahdanau et al. (2014) used a small neural network ('additive' attention); Luong et al. (2015) used dot products ('multiplicative' attention). This paper uses a scaled dot product, chosen for speed (Section 3.2.1).
terms.inThisPaper: Left open in ¶28 and filled in by the scaled dot product in ¶31. In ¶130 the authors note that reducing dₖ hurts quality and suggest a more sophisticated compatibility function might help.

terms.short: Multiply two equal-length lists of numbers position by position and add the results; it is large when the vectors point in similar directions.
terms.background: A basic operation of linear algebra. As an attention score it measures similarity between a query and a key. Because modern hardware multiplies matrices extremely fast, dot-product scores for many query-key pairs can be computed in one matrix multiplication.
terms.inThisPaper: The core of the paper's compatibility function. ¶34 prefers dot-product over additive attention for speed; ¶35 and footnote 1 explain why dot products grow with dₖ and need scaling.

terms.short: A function that turns a list of arbitrary scores into positive weights that sum to one, giving much more weight to larger scores.
terms.background: It exponentiates each score and divides by the total. The same formula appears in statistical physics as the Boltzmann distribution; the name 'softmax' is usually credited to John Bridle around 1990, because it is a smooth ('soft') version of picking the maximum. It is the standard final layer for classification, including predicting the next word from a vocabulary.
terms.inThisPaper: Used in attention to turn query-key scores into weights (¶31, Equation 1), and at the decoder's output to give next-token probabilities (¶53). ¶35 worries that very large scores push it into regions with tiny gradients.

terms.short: The lengths of the key vectors (dₖ, also the query length) and value vectors (dᵥ) inside each attention head.
terms.background: Named by this paper as part of its set of dimension symbols; later work kept the notation.
terms.inThisPaper: Both are 64 in the base model (d_model/h = 512/8). The attention scores are divided by √dₖ. Table 3 rows (A) and (B) vary them; ¶130 reports that reducing dₖ hurts quality.

terms.short: Attention whose query-key score comes from a small neural network with one hidden layer, rather than a dot product.
terms.background: Introduced by Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014), and sometimes called Bahdanau attention. It was the first widely used attention mechanism in neural machine translation.
terms.inThisPaper: Discussed in ¶34–¶35 as the main alternative. The authors grant that it matches dot-product attention in theoretical cost and, per Britz et al. [3], does better than unscaled dot products with large dₖ, but choose dot products for practical speed, with scaling as the fix.

terms.short: How much the model's error would change if a given parameter changed slightly; training follows gradients to reduce the error.
terms.background: Neural networks are trained by gradient descent, with gradients computed by backpropagation. When gradients become extremely small ("vanishing"), learning slows or stalls, a long-standing problem in deep and recurrent networks.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶35 argues that large dot products push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, which motivates the 1/√dₖ scaling.

terms.short: Multiplying a vector by a matrix to map it into a space of possibly different size; with a learned matrix, the model chooses what information to keep.
terms.background: Linear maps are the basic building block of neural networks: a 'layer' is typically a linear transformation followed by a simple non-linear function. On their own, stacked linear maps collapse into a single linear map, which is why networks interleave them with non-linearities such as ReLU. The weights of the matrix are what training adjusts.
terms.inThisPaper: Each head projects queries, keys and values with its own learned matrices (Wᵢ^Q, Wᵢ^K, Wᵢ^V) and the concatenated heads are projected back with Wᴼ. The feed-forward network is two linear transformations with a ReLU between them.

terms.short: A lower-dimensional "view" of the model's vectors, picked out by a projection, in which some kinds of information are emphasised.
terms.background: "Subspace" is linear-algebra vocabulary for a space contained within a larger one. In machine learning, "representation" means the vectors a model uses internally to encode inputs.
terms.inThisPaper: Used in ¶38 to explain multi-head attention: each head works in a different subspace, so the model can attend to different kinds of information at once.

terms.short: Joining vectors end to end to form one longer vector.
terms.background: A standard operation for combining several outputs in neural networks.
terms.inThisPaper: The 8 head outputs, each 64 numbers long, are concatenated into 512 numbers and multiplied by Wᴼ (¶37, ¶39).

terms.short: A table of numbers the model learns during training; together these are the model's parameters (weights).
terms.background: A model's size is often quoted as its number of parameters. They are set by training rather than by hand, in contrast to hyperparameters like the number of layers.
terms.inThisPaper: The projections Wᵢ^Q, Wᵢ^K, Wᵢ^V and Wᴼ (¶41), and W₁, W₂ in the feed-forward network. Table 3 lists parameter counts: 65 million for the base model, 213 million for the big one.

terms.short: Notation for the set of all a-by-b tables (matrices) of real numbers; W ∈ ℝ^(a × b) says W is such a matrix.
terms.background: ℝ is the standard mathematical symbol for the real numbers, and ∈ means "is a member of". Writing ℝ^(a × b) is a compact way to state a matrix's shape.
terms.inThisPaper: Used in ¶41 to give the shapes of the projection matrices and in section 4 for vectors in ℝᵈ.

terms.short: Attention in which the decoder's queries look at keys and values from the encoder's output, letting each output position consult the whole input.
terms.background: This is the kind of attention introduced for translation by Bahdanau et al. (2014) and used in later systems such as Google's GNMT and ConvS2S. Later literature usually calls it cross-attention.
terms.inThisPaper: The third sub-layer in each decoder layer (¶26, ¶45), described as mimicking earlier sequence-to-sequence models [38, 2, 9].

terms.short: A model that maps one sequence (such as a sentence) to another (such as its translation), usually with an encoder and a decoder.
terms.background: The approach was popularised in 2014 by Sutskever, Vinyals and Le, and by Cho et al., using recurrent neural networks; attention (Bahdanau et al.) was soon added so the decoder could look back at the input. It became the standard design for machine translation before the Transformer. "Seq2seq" is the common abbreviation. The Transformer is itself a sequence-to-sequence model, but without recurrence.
terms.inThisPaper: Cited in ¶45 as the source of encoder-decoder attention, and in ¶132 and ¶150, where RNN sequence-to-sequence models serve as a comparison for parsing.

terms.short: Rectified linear unit: a function that leaves positive numbers unchanged and turns negatives into zero.
terms.background: An activation function supplies the non-linearity that lets a network model more than straight-line relationships. ReLU became the default in deep learning around 2010–2012, notably after Nair and Hinton (2010) and its use in image networks, because it is cheap and eases gradient flow.
terms.inThisPaper: Sits between the two linear transformations of the feed-forward network, written max(0, xW₁ + b₁) in Equation 2.

terms.short: A convolution that looks at only one position at a time, so it applies the same transformation to each position independently.
terms.background: Convolutions slide a small learned filter (kernel) along a sequence or image; kernel size is how many neighbouring positions it sees. Size-1 ("1×1") convolutions were popularised in image networks such as Network in Network (Lin et al., 2013) and GoogLeNet to mix channels cheaply.
terms.inThisPaper: Offered in ¶51 as an equivalent description of the position-wise feed-forward network. Elsewhere the paper contrasts its attention-based design with convolutional models such as ConvS2S and ByteNet.

terms.short: The width of the hidden layer inside the feed-forward network.
terms.background: Part of the paper's dimension notation, kept by later work. Setting it about four times d_model became a common default.
terms.inThisPaper: 2,048 in the base model and 4,096 in the big model; Table 3 rows (C) show that a larger d_ff improves results.

terms.short: The basic unit of text a model reads and writes: a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark, depending on how the text was split.
terms.background: In natural language processing, 'tokenisation' is the step of chopping raw text into units. Early translation systems used whole words, which left rare words unknown; since about 2016 most systems use sub-word units such as byte-pair encoding or word-pieces, so any word can be spelt out from smaller pieces. Token counts are now the standard way to measure text length and model cost.
terms.inThisPaper: Tokens are sub-word units from byte-pair encoding (English–German, about 37,000 types) or word-pieces (English–French, 32,000). Batches are sized in tokens (about 25,000 source and 25,000 target, ¶76), and the decoder predicts the next token (¶53).

terms.short: Using one and the same matrix of learned weights for the input embedding and the output layer, instead of learning two separate ones.
terms.background: Proposed for language models in 2016, independently by Press and Wolf (reference [30]) and by Inan, Khosravi and Socher. The idea is that the input lookup and the output scoring both relate tokens to the same vector space, so sharing weights cuts the parameter count and often improves quality. It has become common practice in language models.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶53 shares a single matrix across three places: the encoder's embedding, the decoder's embedding and the pre-softmax output layer. Sharing across encoder and decoder goes a step beyond Press and Wolf's language-model setting and depends on the shared English–German vocabulary (¶76).

terms.short: Producing, at each step, a probability for every possible next token given what has come before.
terms.background: This is how neural language models and translation decoders generate text: predict a distribution, pick a token (for example by beam search), append it, and repeat. The idea goes back to statistical language modelling in speech recognition. It is also the training objective of later large language models.
terms.inThisPaper: The decoder's output passes through a linear layer and softmax to give next-token probabilities (¶53); masking in the decoder (¶47) ensures each prediction only sees earlier tokens.

terms.short: Any layer inside a neural network between the input and the output, whose values are not directly observed.
terms.background: The term dates from early multilayer perceptrons of the 1980s, where 'hidden units' were those neither input nor output. It is now a generic word for an intermediate representation.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶67 uses it to describe the job every candidate layer type does inside an encoder or decoder: map a sequence of n vectors to another sequence of n vectors.

terms.short: Latin for 'things desired': the requirements or wished-for properties used to judge a design.
terms.background: Singular 'desideratum'. It is common in academic writing across fields for a list of criteria a good solution should meet.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶67 introduces three: computation per layer, parallelisability (minimum sequential operations) and maximum path length (¶68–¶69). They are the columns of Table 1.

terms.short: A way of saying how a cost grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors: O(n²) means roughly proportional to the square of n.
terms.background: Introduced in number theory by Paul Bachmann in 1894 and popularised by Edmund Landau, it was adopted by computer science to describe algorithm running time and memory. It captures scaling, not absolute speed: an O(n) method with a large constant can be slower than an O(n²) method on small inputs.
terms.inThisPaper: Table 1 and ¶70–¶71 use it to compare layer types, for example self-attention O(n²·d) against recurrence O(n·d²). O(1) means constant, independent of sentence length.

terms.short: How much arithmetic a method needs, expressed as a function of the input size.
terms.background: A central notion in computer science since the 1960s; for neural networks it is usually counted as the number of multiply-and-add operations. It measures total work, not elapsed time, since work can sometimes be split across many processors.
terms.inThisPaper: The first of the three desiderata (¶68) and the first column of Table 1. ¶70 shows self-attention needs less of it than recurrence when n < d; ¶71 compares convolutions. Training cost in FLOPs appears in Table 2.

terms.short: The number of steps that must be done one after another because each depends on the last; the fewer there are, the more the work can run in parallel.
terms.background: This is the 'depth' of a computation in parallel-computing terms. It matters because GPUs and TPUs are fast only when thousands of operations can run simultaneously; a long chain of dependent steps leaves them idle. Recurrent networks are inherently sequential across time steps, which is why they train slowly on such hardware.
terms.inThisPaper: The paper's measure of parallelisability (¶68) and the middle column of Table 1: O(1) for self-attention and convolution, O(n) for recurrence (¶70). It underpins the claim that the Transformer trains faster (¶5, ¶153).

terms.short: The largest number of steps a signal must pass through in the network to connect any two positions in the sequence.
terms.background: The idea comes from analysis of recurrent networks: when information and training signals must pass through many steps, they tend to fade or blow up (the vanishing and exploding gradient problems), making long-range relationships hard to learn. The reference used here, Hochreiter and colleagues [12], is a classic statement of that difficulty.
terms.inThisPaper: The third desideratum (¶69) and last column of Table 1: O(1) for self-attention, O(n) for recurrence, O(logₖ(n)) for dilated convolutions, O(n/r) for restricted self-attention. The paper treats it as a proxy for how easily long-range dependencies are learned.

terms.short: Self-attention limited so that each position attends only to a window of r nearby positions, which makes the cost grow linearly rather than quadratically with sequence length.
terms.background: Local forms of attention existed before (Luong and colleagues proposed 'local attention' for translation in 2015). Some of this paper's authors used local self-attention soon afterwards in the Image Transformer (2018), and a large later literature on 'sparse' or 'efficient' attention (for example the Sparse Transformer and Longformer) developed the idea for long inputs.
terms.inThisPaper: Proposed in ¶70 and Table 1 as a way to handle very long sequences, with path length rising to O(n/r); not built or tested here, and listed as future work (¶154).

terms.short: A neural-network layer that reads a sequence one item at a time, carrying a running summary (a hidden state) from each step to the next.
terms.background: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) date to the 1980s, notably Elman's 1990 networks. Their improved variants, the LSTM (1997) and GRU (2014), dominated language tasks from about 2014 to 2017, including Google's production translator (reference [38]). Their step-by-step nature makes them hard to parallelise.
terms.inThisPaper: The main architecture the Transformer replaces (¶5, ¶152). In Table 1: O(n·d²) cost, O(n) sequential steps and O(n) path length. ¶70 compares it directly with self-attention.

terms.short: A layer that slides a small window (the kernel, of width k) along the sequence, computing each output from only k neighbouring inputs with the same weights at every position.
terms.background: Convolutional networks were developed for images, notably by Yann LeCun from the late 1980s. From 2016 they were applied to text and translation (ByteNet [18], ConvS2S [9]) because, unlike recurrent networks, every position can be computed at once.
terms.inThisPaper: The second rival in Table 1: O(k·n·d²) cost, O(1) sequential steps, but many stacked layers are needed to link distant words (¶71). ¶51 notes the Transformer's feed-forward layer is equivalent to a convolution with kernel size 1.

terms.short: Convolutions whose window skips over inputs at regular gaps, with the gaps doubling (or otherwise growing) layer by layer, so a few layers can cover a very long stretch.
terms.background: The technique has roots in signal processing (the 'à trous' algorithm for wavelets) and was popularised in deep learning in 2015–16, for example by Yu and Koltun for image segmentation and by DeepMind's WaveNet for audio. ByteNet [18] used it for translation.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶71 and Table 1 use it to give convolutions their best path length, O(logₖ(n)), compared with O(n/k) for ordinary contiguous kernels.

terms.short: A cheaper form of convolution that splits the work in two: first each channel is filtered separately across positions, then the channels are mixed at each position.
terms.background: Known as depthwise separable convolutions, the idea was used in image networks by Laurent Sifre and popularised by François Chollet's Xception (reference [6]) and Google's MobileNets. It cuts cost substantially with little loss of accuracy.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶71 notes it reduces convolution cost to O(k·n·d + n·d²), and that even at k = n this merely equals the cost of the Transformer's self-attention layer plus feed-forward layer.

terms.short: A vector added to each token's embedding that tells the model where in the sequence the token sits.
terms.background: Models built from attention alone treat their input as an unordered set, so word order must be supplied separately. ConvS2S [9] used learned position embeddings; this paper introduced the fixed sine-and-cosine scheme. Later work developed relative position methods (Shaw and colleagues, 2018), rotary embeddings (Su and colleagues, 2021) and ALiBi (Press and colleagues, 2021), partly because the original schemes extrapolate poorly to longer inputs.
terms.inThisPaper: Added to the input embeddings at the bottom of both stacks (¶61), defined with sinusoids (¶63), chosen for a hoped-for relative-position property (¶64) and for possible extrapolation (¶65). Table 3 row (E) shows learned embeddings perform almost identically.

terms.short: A smooth repeating wave shaped like the sine function; its wavelength is the distance over which it repeats.
terms.background: Sines and cosines are the building blocks of Fourier analysis, which represents any signal as a sum of waves of different frequencies. Using many frequencies at once gives each position a distinctive pattern, much as the hands of a clock together identify a time.
terms.inThisPaper: Each dimension of the positional encoding is a sinusoid, with wavelengths in a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π (¶63–¶64). Because each sine has a cosine partner at the same frequency, shifting position by k is a rotation, which is a linear transformation (¶64).

terms.short: Position vectors that are learned from data like word embeddings, one per position, rather than computed from a fixed formula.
terms.background: Learned position embeddings were used in ConvS2S (Gehring et al., 2017) and later in BERT and the GPT models. Their drawback is that they exist only for positions seen in training, whereas a formula can in principle be applied to any length.
terms.inThisPaper: Tested as an alternative in ¶65; Table 3 row (E) gives 25.7 BLEU against 25.8 for sinusoids, 'nearly identical'.

terms.short: Making predictions outside the range of the data a model was trained on; here, handling sentences longer than any seen in training.
terms.background: In statistics, extrapolation is riskier than interpolation because the model has no evidence about the unseen range. 'Length extrapolation' became an active research topic for Transformers from about 2021, when experiments showed that sinusoidal encodings in fact do not extrapolate well.
terms.inThisPaper: Given in ¶65 as the reason to prefer sinusoidal over learned encodings, hedged with 'may' and not tested in the paper.

terms.short: A way of splitting text into sub-word units chosen so that frequent words stay whole and rare words break into common pieces.
terms.background: Introduced by Schuster and Nakajima (2012) for Japanese and Korean voice search at Google, and used in Google's neural translation system (reference [38]). It is close in spirit to byte-pair encoding but picks merges by how much they improve a language model rather than by raw frequency. BERT later popularised it.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶70 gives word-pieces as an example of representations that keep sentences short relative to d; ¶76 uses a 32,000-unit word-piece vocabulary for English–French. Table 3's perplexities are 'per-wordpiece'.

terms.short: A method that builds a vocabulary of sub-word units by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols in the training text.
terms.background: Byte-pair encoding began as a data-compression method (Gage, 1994) and was adapted for translation by Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2015/2016): it repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols into a new unit. Word-pieces are a similar scheme from Google (Schuster and Nakajima, 2012), used in GNMT. Sub-word vocabularies are now standard in language models.
terms.inThisPaper: Used for English–German with a shared source–target vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens (¶76), which is what allows one embedding matrix for both languages (¶53). In ¶76 the citation is to Britz and colleagues [3] rather than to Sennrich [31], who is cited for it in ¶70.

terms.short: A sentence together with its translation, the basic training example for machine translation.
terms.background: Collections of such pairs are called parallel corpora; they come from sources such as parliamentary proceedings, news and web text. Translation models learn entirely from them.
terms.inThisPaper: WMT 2014 English–German has about 4.5 million; batches are built from pairs of similar length (¶76).

terms.short: One of several attention operations run side by side in a layer, each with its own learned weights; its 'attention distribution' is the set of weights showing how much each word attends to every other.
terms.background: Multi-head attention was introduced in this paper (Section 3.2.2). Inspecting heads became a popular way of trying to understand Transformers, though whether attention weights explain model behaviour was later disputed, notably in 'Attention is not Explanation' (Jain and Wallace, 2019) and the reply 'Attention is not not Explanation' (Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019).
terms.inThisPaper: The base model has 8 heads per layer, the big model 16 (Table 3). ¶72 and the appendix (¶200–¶202) claim heads specialise in different tasks, including sentence structure and pronoun reference.

terms.short: How far people can understand why a model produces the outputs it does.
terms.background: A long-standing concern in machine learning that grew into its own research area as deep networks became more powerful and opaque. Methods range from inspecting internal weights and activations to probing experiments; later 'mechanistic interpretability' work studies Transformers' internal circuits in detail.
terms.inThisPaper: Offered in ¶72 as a 'side benefit' of self-attention, with evidence from attention visualisations in the appendix.

terms.short: One update of a model's weights, made after processing one batch of training examples.
terms.background: Neural networks learn by repeatedly showing the model a batch of examples, measuring its errors, and nudging every weight to reduce them. Each such nudge is one step. Training length is usually reported in steps rather than passes over the data, especially when batch sizes are fixed by token count, as here. The learning rate is often set as a function of the step number.
terms.inThisPaper: The base model trains for 100,000 steps and the big model for 300,000 (¶78, Table 3). Each batch holds about 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens (¶76). The learning-rate formula (¶81) depends on step_num.

terms.short: A setting chosen by the researchers before training, such as layer count or learning rate, as opposed to the weights the model learns itself.
terms.background: In machine learning, 'parameters' are the numbers a model learns from data, while 'hyperparameters' are the design and training choices that shape that learning. They are usually tuned by trying several values and checking results on a development set, not the test set. Results can be sensitive to them, which is one reason reported comparisons between models can be hard to interpret.
terms.inThisPaper: The paper lists its hyperparameters throughout Sections 3 and 5, and Table 3 is essentially a study of how varying them changes quality. Decoding settings were "chosen after experimentation on the development set" (¶103).

terms.short: The paper's standard, smaller Transformer configuration (6 layers, width 512, 8 heads, about 65 million parameters).
terms.background: Machine-learning papers often report a default configuration plus a larger one, so readers can see how results scale with size. This paper's 'base' and 'big' labels were adopted widely afterwards: later models such as BERT also came in 'base' and 'large' sizes. The base model serves as the reference point that ablation studies vary.
terms.inThisPaper: Its settings are the first row of Table 3 (¶109). It trains in about 12 hours (¶78) and already beats all earlier English-to-German systems (¶101).

terms.short: The paper's larger Transformer configuration (width 1024, feed-forward width 4096, 16 heads, about 213 million parameters).
terms.background: Scaling a network up, making it wider, deeper or both, is a standard way to improve quality at the cost of more computation. This paper's result that the bigger configuration does better foreshadowed the later trend of scaling Transformers to billions of parameters.
terms.inThisPaper: Its configuration is the last row of Table 3 (¶128). It trains for 3.5 days (¶78) and produces the headline BLEU scores in Table 2 (¶98, ¶101–¶102). For English-to-French it used dropout 0.1 instead of 0.3 (¶102).

terms.short: A widely used method for updating a neural network's weights that adapts the step size for each weight using running averages of its recent gradients.
terms.background: Adam was introduced by Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba (published at ICLR 2015). It combines 'momentum' (keeping a running average of the direction of recent gradients) with per-weight scaling by a running average of squared gradients. β1 and β2 set how quickly these two averages forget old information, and ϵ is a tiny number that prevents division by zero. The usual defaults are β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999 and ϵ = 10⁻⁸. Later variants such as AdamW changed how weight decay is handled.
terms.inThisPaper: Used with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10⁻⁹ (¶80): a lower β2 than the default, so the size estimates react faster to recent gradients.

terms.short: How big a step the optimiser takes when adjusting the weights after each batch.
terms.background: Too high a learning rate makes training unstable; too low makes it slow or leaves it stuck. Rather than using one fixed value, practitioners often use a schedule that changes it over training, commonly decreasing it as training goes on. Choosing the schedule is one of the most consequential and fiddly hyperparameter decisions.
terms.inThisPaper: Set by Equation (3) (¶81): a linear warm-up for 4,000 steps, then decay proportional to one over the square root of the step number, scaled by d_model^−0.5 (¶82).

terms.short: Starting training with a very small learning rate and raising it gradually over the first few thousand steps.
terms.background: Early in training, a model's weights are random and its gradients can be large and erratic; full-size steps then can derail training. Warm-up avoids this by ramping the learning rate up. The specific schedule in this paper, warm-up followed by inverse-square-root decay, became known in software libraries as the 'Noam' schedule, after co-author Noam Shazeer. Later research (for example Xiong et al., 2020) linked the need for warm-up in Transformers partly to where layer normalisation is placed.
terms.inThisPaper: The learning rate rises linearly for warmup_steps = 4000 steps, then decays (¶81–¶82).

terms.short: Any technique that discourages a model from memorising its training data, so it performs better on new data.
terms.background: A flexible model with many parameters can fit quirks and noise in its training data that do not generalise, a problem called over-fitting. Regularisation methods counter this by adding noise, penalties or constraints during training. Classic examples include penalising large weights (weight decay), dropout, and stopping training early.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶84 promises three types but describes two: residual dropout (¶85) and label smoothing (¶86). Their effects are tested in Table 3 rows (D).

terms.short: A regularisation technique that randomly switches off a fraction of a network's units during each training step.
terms.background: Dropout was introduced by Geoffrey Hinton's group in Toronto (a 2012 preprint, then Srivastava et al., 2014, in the Journal of Machine Learning Research). By randomly removing units, it stops the network relying on any single pathway, and it can be seen as cheaply training many overlapping sub-networks. At test time nothing is dropped. It became one of the most common regularisers in deep learning.
terms.inThisPaper: Applied to each sub-layer's output before the residual addition and normalisation, and to the embeddings-plus-positional-encodings sum (¶85): hence 'residual dropout'. The rate P_drop is 0.1 for the base model and 0.3 for the big one (¶128), except 0.1 for the big English-to-French model (¶102). Table 3 shows that removing it hurts (¶123, ¶130).

terms.short: Training the model against softened targets, for example 90% on the correct word and the remaining 10% spread over the other words, instead of 100% on the correct word.
terms.background: Label smoothing was introduced by Szegedy et al. (2015) in their work on the Inception image-classification network. It discourages the model from becoming over-confident, which tends to improve accuracy and makes its probability estimates better calibrated. Later analysis (Müller, Kornblith and Hinton, 2019) examined when it helps and noted side effects, such as making the network less useful as a 'teacher' for training other models.
terms.inThisPaper: Used with ε_ls = 0.1 (¶86). The paper notes that it worsens perplexity but improves BLEU, which Table 3 rows (D) confirm (¶125–¶126).

terms.short: A measure of how surprised a language model is by the correct text; lower is better.
terms.background: Perplexity comes from information theory and has long been the standard measure for language models in speech recognition and natural language processing. It is the exponential of the average negative log-probability the model assigns to each correct token, and can be read as the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively picking between. Its value depends on the unit of text, so per-word and per-sub-word perplexities are not comparable.
terms.inThisPaper: Reported per word-piece in Table 3 on the development set, with an explicit warning not to compare it with per-word figures (¶107). Label smoothing makes it worse while improving BLEU (¶86, ¶125).

terms.short: Floating-point operations: a count of arithmetic operations on decimal numbers, used here as a hardware-neutral measure of training cost.
terms.background: Counting total operations lets papers compare training cost across different hardware and run times. It is easily confused with FLOPS, operations per second, a measure of hardware speed; footnote 2 uses TFLOPS, trillions per second. Since this paper, reporting training compute in FLOPs has become common, especially in work on how model quality scales with compute.
terms.inThisPaper: Estimated as training time × number of GPUs × assumed sustained speed per GPU (¶104), with 9.5 TFLOPS for the P100 (footnote 2, ¶204). The Transformer's estimates are 3.3·10¹⁸ (base) and 2.3·10¹⁹ (big).

terms.short: The standard 32-bit format computers use to store decimal numbers; a GPU's single-precision capacity is how many such operations it can do per second.
terms.background: Floating-point numbers store a value as digits plus an exponent, like scientific notation. Single precision uses 32 bits; double precision uses 64 and is more exact but slower. Deep learning has since moved largely to 16-bit and even 8-bit formats, which are faster still. A chip's 'sustained' capacity is what it can keep up in practice, below its theoretical peak.
terms.inThisPaper: The cost estimate assumes each GPU delivers its sustained single-precision capacity for the whole of training (¶104).

terms.short: The official test set of news sentences for the 2014 Workshop on Machine Translation (WMT) shared tasks, a standard benchmark for English–German and English–French translation.
terms.background: WMT, now the Conference on Machine Translation, has run annual 'shared tasks' since 2006, in which teams translate the same held-out news texts so results can be compared directly. Each year's test set is named 'newstest' plus the year. The 2014 English–German and English–French tasks became the standard benchmarks for neural translation papers in the following years.
terms.inThisPaper: Table 2's scores are on newstest2014 (¶87); the training data are also from WMT 2014 (¶76).

terms.short: A held-out portion of data used to tune choices during research, kept separate from the final test set.
terms.background: Good practice in machine learning splits data three ways: a training set to learn from, a development (or validation) set for choosing hyperparameters, and a test set touched only for the final report. Tuning on the test set inflates results, because choices get fitted to its quirks. For WMT, the previous year's test set is often used as the development set.
terms.inThisPaper: The authors tuned decoding settings on the development set (¶103) and report all Table 3 variations on newstest2013 (¶106–¶107).

terms.short: Averaging the weights saved at several points late in training to make one final model.
terms.background: During training, models are saved periodically as 'checkpoints'. Averaging the weights of the last few tends to smooth out the noise of individual updates and gives a small, free gain. It is related to older ideas of averaging parameters along the optimisation path, and is a cheaper cousin of ensembling, since it yields one model rather than several.
terms.inThisPaper: The base model averages the last 5 checkpoints (saved every 10 minutes) and the big model the last 20 (¶103). Table 3 does not use it (¶106).

terms.short: A way of generating output that keeps the few most promising partial translations at each step instead of just the single best word.
terms.background: A translation model produces text one word-piece at a time. Always picking the likeliest next piece ('greedy' decoding) can lead into dead ends; trying every possibility is impossible. Beam search is the compromise: it keeps a fixed number (the beam size) of best partial outputs, extends each, and keeps the best again. It dates back to early speech-recognition and AI search work and became the default decoding method in neural translation.
terms.inThisPaper: Used with a beam size of 4 and a length penalty α = 0.6, following GNMT [38] (¶103); also used in Table 3 (¶106).

terms.short: An adjustment to beam search scores that stops the search from unfairly favouring short outputs.
terms.background: Because each extra word multiplies in another probability below one, shorter translations naturally score higher, biasing beam search towards truncated output. A length penalty normalises scores by a function of length. The version cited here comes from Google's GNMT system (Wu et al., 2016), where α controls the strength of the correction.
terms.inThisPaper: α = 0.6, borrowed from GNMT (¶103).

terms.short: Using a trained model to produce outputs, as distinct from training it.
terms.background: In machine learning, 'inference' means running the model forward on new inputs. This is different from the statistical sense of inferring conclusions from data. Inference cost matters for deployment and is often reported separately from training cost.
terms.inThisPaper: Output length is capped at input length plus 50 during inference, with early stopping when possible (¶103).

terms.short: A deep recurrent translation model from Baidu (Deep-Att) combined with a technique for handling unknown words (PosUnk).
terms.background: Zhou et al. (2016) built very deep stacks of LSTM layers with 'fast-forward' shortcut connections. PosUnk refers to a method for rare words, associated with Luong and colleagues (2015), that records the source position of words the model cannot translate, so they can be filled in afterwards.
terms.inThisPaper: A baseline for English-to-French in Table 2, as a single model (39.2) and an ensemble (40.4) (¶90, ¶94).

terms.short: Google's Neural Machine Translation system: a large recurrent (LSTM) encoder–decoder with attention, deployed in Google Translate from 2016.
terms.background: Described by Wu et al. (2016), GNMT used deep stacks of LSTM layers, attention, and word-piece vocabularies, and was notable as a production-scale neural translation system. '+ RL' refers to an extra stage in which the model was fine-tuned with reinforcement learning towards a BLEU-like reward. It was the main recurrent system that the Transformer, also from Google, sought to replace.
terms.inThisPaper: A baseline in Table 2 (¶91, ¶95), and the source of the beam-search settings (¶103) and the word-piece vocabulary (¶76).

terms.short: Mixture of experts: a model made of many sub-networks ('experts') in which a gating network sends each input to only a few of them.
terms.background: The mixture-of-experts idea dates to the early 1990s (Jacobs, Jordan and colleagues). Shazeer et al. (2017) scaled it up with a 'sparsely gated' layer inside an LSTM model, so total capacity could grow enormously while the computation per word stayed modest. Sparse mixtures of experts later returned in very large Transformer-based language models.
terms.inThisPaper: In Table 2, the best previous single model on both language pairs (26.03 and 40.56, ¶93).

terms.short: The lengths of the key and value vectors each attention head works with.
terms.background: In attention, each word produces a query, a key and a value. A query is compared with every key to decide how much weight to give each value. The dimensions dₖ and dᵥ are the paper's notation (Section 3.2); larger ones give each head more room to represent information.
terms.inThisPaper: Base setting dₖ = dᵥ = 64 (¶42). Rows (A) change them together with the head count; rows (B) shrink dₖ alone, which hurts quality (¶114–¶115, ¶130).

terms.short: The learned numbers (weights) inside a model; their count is a rough measure of its size.
terms.background: A neural network's behaviour is set by its parameters, which training adjusts. Parameter count is the most common shorthand for model size, although computation per input can differ greatly between models of the same size (mixture-of-experts models are an example).
terms.inThisPaper: Table 3 lists counts in millions: 65 for base, 213 for big, 28 to 168 for variants (¶108–¶128).

terms.short: When a model learns its training data too closely, including noise, and so does worse on new data.
terms.background: Over-fitting is a central problem in statistics and machine learning: a model with enough capacity can memorise rather than generalise. It is detected by comparing performance on training data with performance on held-out data, and countered by regularisation, more data, or smaller models.
terms.inThisPaper: Dropout is "very helpful in avoiding over-fitting" (¶130), as rows (D) show (¶123).

terms.short: The paper's fixed, non-learned signal of word position, built from sine and cosine waves of different frequencies and added to each word's vector.
terms.background: Because attention by itself ignores word order, the model needs position information added in. This paper introduced the sinusoidal scheme (Section 3.5). Many later models switched to learned embeddings (BERT, GPT) or to relative schemes such as rotary position embeddings (RoPE, Su et al., 2021).
terms.inThisPaper: The default (¶61–¶65); ¶85 applies dropout to the sum of embeddings and positional encodings. Row (E) shows learned embeddings do about as well (¶127, ¶130).

terms.short: Whether a model or architecture that works on one task also works well on different tasks, or on data it was not trained on.
terms.background: In machine learning, "generalisation" has two related senses: a trained model performing well on unseen examples of the same task, and an architecture transferring to new tasks. The second sense matters when judging whether a design is general-purpose or tailored to one problem. Claims of generality are usually supported by testing on a task deliberately unlike the original one.
terms.inThisPaper: Used in the second sense: Section 6.3 tests whether the architecture, designed for translation, also handles parsing (¶132, ¶135).

terms.short: A setting where only a limited amount of labelled training data is available.
terms.background: Neural networks typically need large amounts of data, and results in small-data settings often favour older methods that build in more prior knowledge. "Regime" is borrowed from physics and just means a range of conditions. Performance in small-data regimes is a common test of how data-efficient an architecture is.
terms.inThisPaper: The WSJ-only setting (about 40,000 sentences) is the small-data regime of Section 6.3, where RNN seq2seq models fell short (¶132) but the Transformer did well (¶150).

aliases: Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank
terms.short: A large collection of English sentences hand-annotated with their phrase-structure trees, the standard dataset for training and testing English parsers.
terms.background: Built at the University of Pennsylvania and described by Marcus, Marcinkiewicz and Santorini (1993). Its Wall Street Journal portion, about a million words of 1989 newspaper text, is divided into numbered sections. By convention, sections 2–21 are used for training, section 22 for development (tuning) and section 23 for the final test, so results across papers are comparable.
terms.inThisPaper: The source of the roughly 40K training sentences (¶133); Section 22 is used for tuning (¶134) and Section 23 for the reported scores in Table 4.

terms.short: Training with a small amount of carefully labelled data plus a large amount of data that is unlabelled or labelled automatically.
terms.background: Semi-supervised methods try to exploit the abundance of raw text when human annotation is expensive. In parsing, a common form is self-training: parse lots of new text with an existing parser and train on the output (McClosky et al. 2006). Vinyals et al. (2015) built a large corpus of automatically parsed sentences for the same purpose. The term is used loosely; strictly, training on machine-generated labels is sometimes called "silver" data as opposed to human "gold" data.
terms.inThisPaper: The second condition of Section 6.3: the Transformer is also trained on about 17M machine-parsed sentences from [37] (¶133), reaching 92.7 F1 (¶146).

terms.short: A semi-supervised method where a model labels new data itself and is then retrained on those labels.
terms.background: Self-training is an old idea in machine learning. For a long time it was thought not to help parsers, until McClosky, Charniak and Johnson (2006) showed it did when a reranker was used to pick the parses. Huang and Harper (2009) applied it to grammars with latent annotations.
terms.inThisPaper: Appears in the titles of the cited works [14] and [26], the semi-supervised baselines in Table 4 (¶143, ¶144).

terms.short: A large set of automatically parsed sentences kept only where the parse is likely to be right, used as extra training data.
terms.background: Vinyals et al. (2015) built extra training data for their neural parser by running existing parsers over large amounts of unannotated text; as the name suggests, the high-confidence corpus keeps sentences whose automatic parses are judged reliable (they used agreement between parsers as the test). They also used a corpus parsed by the BerkeleyParser alone.
terms.inThisPaper: The source of the roughly 17M sentences in the semi-supervised setting (¶133). The paper spells the parser's name "BerkleyParser" here.

terms.short: A widely used statistical constituency parser developed at the University of California, Berkeley.
terms.background: It implements the approach of Petrov, Barrett, Thibaux and Klein (2006), which learns finer-grained grammar categories automatically by splitting and merging treebank labels. It was one of the strongest and most-used English parsers of the late 2000s. It serves both as a baseline and as a tool for generating automatic parses.
terms.inThisPaper: Named in ¶133 (as "BerkleyParser") as the source of one extra corpus, and in ¶150 as the parser the Transformer beats with WSJ data alone (91.3 against 90.4).

terms.short: Adjusting a model's design or settings specifically for one task to get the best result on it.
terms.background: Much of the progress on benchmarks comes from such tuning, so a model that does well with little of it is taken as evidence of a robust, general design. The boundary between light and heavy tuning is not sharp.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶149 claims the Transformer did well "despite the lack of task-specific tuning", though ¶134 reports tuning of dropout, learning rates and beam size.

terms.short: A single accuracy score combining precision (how many of the predicted items are right) and recall (how many of the right items were found), as their harmonic mean.
terms.background: F1 is widely used in information retrieval and NLP. For constituency parsing it is computed over labelled brackets: each predicted phrase with its label and span is checked against the gold-standard tree. The standard scoring tool is EVALB. Scores are out of 100, and by the mid-2010s top parsers were above 90.
terms.inThisPaper: The metric in Table 4, on WSJ Section 23 (¶136). The Transformer scores 91.3 (WSJ only) and 92.7 (semi-supervised).

terms.short: A discriminative parser learns to predict the tree given the sentence; a generative parser models how the sentence and tree are produced together.
terms.background: The distinction comes from statistics and machine learning: discriminative models learn the conditional probability of an answer given the input, while generative models learn the joint probability of both. Generative models can be more data-efficient but are often harder to use for search, so they are frequently used to rescore candidates from another parser.
terms.inThisPaper: The "Training" column of Table 4 labels most systems discriminative; only Dyer et al.'s generative RNNG (93.3, ¶148) is marked generative, and it has the best score.

terms.short: A neural parser that builds a sentence's tree step by step with a recurrent network, explicitly modelling the phrase structure.
terms.background: Introduced by Dyer, Kuncoro, Ballesteros and Smith (2016). Unlike seq2seq parsers, it has syntax built into its design, composing phrases as it goes. It comes in a discriminative and a generative version, the latter giving the best result in Table 4.
terms.inThisPaper: The one model family the authors concede beats the Transformer on parsing (¶149, Table 4 rows ¶140 and ¶148).

terms.short: Training one model on several tasks at once so that what it learns for one helps the others.
terms.background: The idea was set out by Caruana in the 1990s. Luong et al. (2015) trained sequence-to-sequence models on translation, parsing and other tasks together. Multi-task results are not directly comparable with single-task ones because the model sees more data.
terms.inThisPaper: Luong et al.'s multi-task model scores 93.0 in Table 4 (¶147), above the Transformer, though ¶149 does not mention it as an exception.

terms.short: Probabilistic context-free grammar: a set of phrase-structure rules, each with a probability, used to score possible trees for a sentence.
terms.background: Context-free grammars come from Chomsky's formal language theory; attaching probabilities to rules made them the basis of statistical parsing in the 1990s. Plain treebank PCFGs are weak, so later work refined the categories, for example with automatically learned "latent annotations" (Petrov et al. 2006).
terms.inThisPaper: Appears only in the title of the cited work [14] behind the semi-supervised baseline in ¶143.

terms.short: A parsing method that reads a sentence left to right, either moving the next word onto a stack (shift) or combining items on the stack into a phrase (reduce).
terms.background: Shift-reduce parsing comes from compiler design and was adapted to natural language with statistical models choosing each action. It is fast because it makes one pass through the sentence. Zhu et al. (2013) made it competitive in accuracy for constituency parsing.
terms.inThisPaper: Named only in the title of [40], the Zhu et al. baseline in Table 4 (¶139, ¶142).

terms.short: A design where one part of a network (the encoder) turns the input into internal representations and another (the decoder) generates the output from them.
terms.background: Common in translation since 2014; the encoder and decoder were usually recurrent networks linked by attention. The Transformer keeps this overall shape but builds both halves from attention and feed-forward layers.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶152 describes the Transformer as keeping the encoder-decoder design while replacing its recurrent layers with multi-headed self-attention (see Section 3.1).

terms.short: A kind of data, such as text, images, audio or video.
terms.background: In machine learning, "multimodal" systems handle more than one kind of data. Different modalities pose different problems: images and audio produce much longer input sequences than sentences.
terms.inThisPaper: ¶154 plans to extend the Transformer to inputs and outputs other than text.

terms.short: Attention in which each position looks only at a nearby window of positions rather than the whole sequence, to save computation on long inputs.
terms.background: Full self-attention's cost grows with the square of sequence length, which becomes prohibitive for images, audio or long documents. Limiting attention to a neighbourhood of size r cuts the cost at the expense of longer paths between distant positions. Many later "efficient Transformer" designs build on this idea.
terms.inThisPaper: Analysed in Table 1 (¶59) and ¶70; ¶154 names it as a direction for handling images, audio and video.

terms.short: A grammatical relation between words that are far apart in a sentence, such as a verb and the words that complete its phrase.
terms.background: Long-distance dependencies are a classic problem in linguistics and a known weakness of recurrent networks, which must carry information across many steps. The paper's Section 4 argues self-attention handles them better because any two positions are connected in one step.
terms.inThisPaper: Figure 3 (¶200) shows attention heads linking "making" to the distant "more difficult".

terms.short: Working out what an earlier expression a word such as a pronoun refers back to, for example what "its" refers to.
terms.background: Anaphora (Greek for "carrying back") is an expression whose meaning depends on an earlier one. Resolving it, often called coreference resolution in NLP, is a long-standing hard problem because it can depend on meaning and world knowledge, not just grammar.
terms.inThisPaper: Figure 4 (¶201) suggests two heads are "apparently involved" in it, a hedged interpretation of the attention pattern.

terms.short: Drawing the attention weights between words as lines or heat maps to see which words a model links.
terms.background: Attention maps became a popular way to peek inside neural models after attention was introduced. Whether they explain model behaviour is contested: Jain and Wallace (2019) argued attention is often not a faithful explanation, and Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) replied that it can be under some conditions.
terms.inThisPaper: The appendix (¶199–¶202) uses them to argue individual heads learn linguistically meaningful tasks.

terms.short: A measure of how spread out a random quantity's values are around its average; its square root is the standard deviation.
terms.background: A basic idea in probability. A useful fact: when you add up independent random quantities, their variances add. So a sum of dₖ independent terms each with variance 1 has variance dₖ, and a typical size (standard deviation) of √dₖ.
terms.inThisPaper: Footnote 1 (¶203) uses this to show why dot products grow with dₖ and so why attention divides them by √dₖ (¶35).

terms.short: Trillions of floating-point operations per second: a measure of how fast a processor does arithmetic on decimal numbers.
terms.background: FLOPS counts operations on floating-point (decimal) numbers per second; tera- means a trillion. Hardware makers quote peak figures, which real workloads rarely reach. Total floating-point operations are a common hardware-neutral way to compare training costs.
terms.inThisPaper: Footnote 2 (¶204) lists the assumed rates for four GPUs, used in ¶104 to estimate training cost for Table 2.
